• Polars stays below 2.0: the requirement is now polars>=1.41,<2. Polars 2.0 runs lazy queries on the streaming engine by default, which does not keep the row order of joins, and it removes the cast from a string to a date. Fleet moves to Polars 2.0 after its tests pass on it.
  • Python 3.12 to 3.14, httpx below 1.0: the requirements are now requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.15" and httpx>=0.27,<1. On Python 3.15, Polars 1.x Series methods return None, so import fleet now stops there with an ImportError that gives a working command. httpx 1.0 pre-releases change the Client constructor, and a --pre install picked them up, so fleet install-engine and the CDISC Library commands stopped with a TypeError.
  • Spec parameter facts are checked against the verb signature (ADR-0007, #179 phase 1) — the parity test now compares every Param of a spec algorithm with inspect.signature() of its verb: the spec may be stricter than the verb, never looser. The ten spec-only defaults are gone, so a define.yaml must state aval, low and high for nrind, the three dates for on_treatment, term_var for atoxgr, on for merge and lookup, and agg for group_by; ct_codelist is required on assign_ct and hardcode_ct, as the define.yaml concept doc already stated. A missing key is a load-time error

  • One validation HTML page: fleet validate --report and ValidationResult.save_html_report() write the same page (fleet.validation.models.write_html_report()): a status row per dataset, then one row per finding. Every cell is HTML-escaped, so a < in a data value or a custom rule message no longer breaks the page or injects markup; rows_affected=0 is shown (#119)

  • API simplification: therapeutic-area namespaces (onco, ophtha, peds, vaccine, metabolic, neuro) and ADaM sub-structures (adsl, occds) are now accessed via df.adam.<name> instead of df.<name> — reduces registered namespaces from 10 to 2 (df.sdtm and df.adam)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Define-XML FormalExpression names the method the run records: the verb the algorithm dispatches to, by the class that defines it on the define's own namespace, as VariableNode.method does (the fleet lsp hover names the defining class too). ADaM defines named SDTMNamespace and rendered calls that do not exist, such as study_day('ADY', end=..., start=...); ADY now reads fleet.core._verb_mixin.SharedVerbsMixin.duration('ADY', end='ASTDT', start='TRTSDT') (#93)

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• df.sdtm namespace — 14 SDTM derivation verbs
  • df.adam namespace — 22 ADaM BDS derivation verbs, with df.adam.adsl (8 patient-level verbs), df.adam.occds (5 occurrence verbs), and 6 TA extensions
  • Define-XML 2.1 generation from define.yaml
  • Define-XML validation against CDISC schema
  • Controlled terminology loading and validation
  • StudyContext and PipelineDAG for spec-driven pipelines
  • CDISCPILOT01 example dataset and pipeline
  • Pytest suite with fixtures

docs.title: Run the test suite locally
docs.text:
# Install dev dependencies
uv sync --extra dev

# Run all tests
uv run pytest

# With coverage report
uv run pytest --cov=fleet --cov-report=term-missing

docs.title: CI status
docs.text:
GitHub Actions runs these checks:

  • Every pull request and every push to main (ci.yml): ruff, the docs formatter, the generated-reference checks and the tests on Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 (each leg checks that it runs the Python in its name). The 3.12 leg installs every extra, so the LSP, MCP, migrate and render tests run, and it runs the eight example scripts.
  • Weekly and before each release (fresh-install.yml): the built wheel is installed with no lock file, as a user gets it, and the tests and examples run against the installed package.
  • Weekly (admiral-oracle.yml): a grid of real ADAE shapes runs through admiral 1.4.1 and through Fleet, and every cell is compared.
  • Weekly (core-canary.yml): validation runs on the newest CDISC CORE release.

docs.title: Test structure
docs.text: The tests sit in tests/unit, one file per module or finding group, with shared fixtures in tests/conftest.py and sample files in tests/fixtures/. Run uv run pytest --collect-only -q for the current list.

docs.title: Coverage targets
docs.text:
These are goals. CI does not enforce them; run the coverage report above to see the current values.

Module Target sdtm ≥ 90% adam ≥ 90% adsl ≥ 90% define_xml ≥ 85% ct ≥ 85%

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text: Fleet is a Python library that generates CDISC SDTM and ADaM datasets for clinical statistical programming. It is built entirely on Polars through a namespace extension API, and is designed to run inside a sponsor's existing validated Python infrastructure. This document defines Fleet's validation strategy using the risk-based framework established by the R Validation Hub and the software-agnostic regulatory context articulated by the FDA. The strategy is structured around five complementary pillars: standards traceability through the CDISC Library API, cross-language benchmark parity against {admiral}, regulatory-grade validation via the official CDISC Rules Engine (CORE), automated unit testing with static analysis, and a local snapshot of the CORE rules.

docs.title: 2.1 FDA Position on Statistical Software
docs.text:
The FDA's 2015 Statistical Software Clarifying Statement[^1] explicitly states that the agency does not require nor endorse any specific software for analyzing data from clinical investigations. Sponsors are responsible for ensuring that any software used produces accurate results and for maintaining adequate documentation of that accuracy. This places the validation obligation on the sponsor's qualified infrastructure — of which Fleet is one component — rather than on the software vendor alone.

Implication for Fleet

Fleet does not need to be independently validated by a regulatory body. Sponsors qualify Fleet by demonstrating it produces accurate, traceable, and reproducible CDISC-compliant outputs within their own validated environment.

docs.title: 2.2 R Validation Hub Framework
docs.text:
The R Validation Hub white paper[^2] — co-authored by representatives from AstraZeneca, GSK, Roche/Genentech, Amgen, and other sponsors — establishes a risk-based approach for assessing package accuracy within validated infrastructure. Although written for R, the framework is language-agnostic and is increasingly applied to Python packages used in regulatory submissions. The framework classifies packages into three risk tiers based on:

Risk Factor Description Intended use How directly the package generates submission-ready outputs Consequence of inaccuracy Patient safety risk and regulatory impact if results are wrong Testability Availability of unit tests, cross-validation tools, and independent benchmarks

Fleet addresses all three dimensions, as documented in the qualification summary in §5.

docs.title: Pillar 1 — CDISC Library Traceability
docs.text:
Fleet's fleet init define and fleet init ct CLI commands query the CDISC Library REST API[^3] directly to bootstrap study specifications and controlled terminology. Variable metadata (labels, types, core designations, permitted terms) is sourced from the authoritative CDISC machine-readable IG model — not hard-coded. The resulting define.yaml and codelists.py are committed artefacts that provide full lineage from source variable to CDISC standard.

# Step 1: Pull domain variable metadata from the CDISC Library IG for SDTM 3.4
uv run fleet init define

# Step 2: Generate codelists.py from NCI concept IDs in define.yaml
uv run fleet init ct

This produces codelist classes — for example SEX (C66731), RACE (C74457) — that are used in pipeline code by class name, never raw string ID:

from examples.cdiscpilot01.sdtm.codelists import SEX, RACE

dm = (
    raw_df.sdtm.assign("SEX", source="sex", ct=SEX)
    .assign("RACE", source="race", ct=RACE)
    .to_frame()
)

Traceability chain: CDISC Library API → define.yaml → codelists.py → pipeline code → output dataset

Each link is a versioned, reviewable artefact stored alongside the study specification.

docs.title: Pillar 2 — Cross-Language Benchmark: {admiral} Parity
docs.text:
{admiral}[^4] is the R package for ADaM derivations developed by Roche and GSK with the pharmaverse community; it is the de-facto gold standard in R-based clinical programming and is documented in multiple regulatory submissions. Fleet's test suite contains tests/unit/test_admiral_parity.py: 39 tests that check selected {admiral} formulas and patterns, adapted to Polars, against expected values written into the tests. They do not cover every ADaM verb. The known differences are listed below.

Coverage as of v0.1.0:

Test class Algorithms verified TestBSA DuBois, Mosteller, Haycock, Gehan-George (4 methods) TestMeanArterialPressure Standard MAP formula TestQTc Bazett, Fridericia (2 methods) TestAgeInYears AGE converted to years from its AGEU unit (years, months, weeks, days) TestDeriveSummaryRecords Mean aggregation by parameter group (BDS record generation) TestDeriveLOCFRecords Last-observation-carried-forward imputation TestDeriveParam BMI derivation from height/weight TestADSLAgeYears Age derivations on ADSL frame TestADSLDerivePeriod Period start, end and planned treatment copied to APxxSDT, APxxEDT and TRTxxP TestANL01FLAdmiralParity restrict_derivation + derive_var_extreme_flag (last-valid-row ANL01FL pattern)

No R runtime is required. The parity tests work in two ways:

  • Formula transcription: selected formulas (BSA, QTc, MAP, age conversion) are written from the {admiral} R source. The tests compare the Fleet result with an expected value that pure Python computes from the same formula, at the number of decimals that the verb keeps. This is the same formula, not a run of {admiral}.
  • Behavioural specification — for higher-level patterns such as ANL01FL flagging, the expected output rows and flag values are transcribed verbatim from {admiral}'s documented examples (the test comments quote the equivalent R code). Fleet's Python implementation is then verified to reproduce that exact output.

This approach means the validation does not depend on an R installation, a specific R version, or rpy2. It covers only the formulas and patterns in the tests. The weekly admiral oracle job (scripts/admiral_oracle.py) runs {admiral} itself on study day, duration, TRTEMFL and ANL01FL.

Known differences from {admiral}:

Class Fleet {admiral} Sign pchg: (AVAL - BASE) / BASE * 100. AVAL -5, BASE -10 gives PCHG -50. derive_var_pchg divides by abs(BASE): the same row gives 50. Rounding bsa keeps 4 decimals, map and qtc keep 2, bmi keeps 1. compute_bsa, compute_map, compute_qtc do not round. Record structure derive_locf_records fills the null values in place and adds no DTYPE. derive_locf_records adds new records with DTYPE = "LOCF". Missing values pchg gives null when BASE is 0. Same: NA when BASE is 0. Units qtc reads RR in ms (ADR-0013). Same: RR in ms. Grading boundary atoxgr CTCAE v5 GGT, high baseline: AVAL = 2 x BASE gives grade 0, as admiral (ADR-0014). The CTCAE text gives grade 1; ALP at the same boundary gives 1. atoxgr_criteria_ctcv5 GGT uses >, ALP uses >=. 
# Example: ANL01FL last-valid-row parity test
# tests/unit/test_admiral_parity.py — TestANL01FLAdmiralParity
#
# Equivalent admiral R pattern (quoted in test docstring):
#   restrict_derivation(advs, derivation = derive_var_extreme_flag,
#     args = params(by_vars = exprs(USUBJID, PARAMCD),
#                   order = exprs(ADT), new_var = ANL01FL, mode = "last"),
#     filter = !is.na(AVAL))

result = bds_frame.adam.flag(
    "ANL01FL",
    criteria="last",
    order_by="ADT",
    by=["USUBJID", "PARAMCD"],
    where='~pl.col("AVAL").is_null()',
).to_frame()
# Only the last non-null-AVAL record per group receives "Y"; all others are null
assert result["ANL01FL"].to_list() == [None, "Y", None, "Y", None, "Y"]

docs.title: Pillar 3 — Official CDISC Rules Engine (CORE)
docs.text: Fleet integrates the official CDISC Rules Engine (CORE)[^5] — the open-source validation binary published by CDISC, which runs CDISC conformance rules and FDA business rules. (ADaM standard/version selection is supported by the engine, but CDISC has not yet published an executable ADaMIG rule set — ADaM validation today runs custom rules; see Validation with CORE.) Fleet manages the engine lifecycle through its own CLI and wraps it via a Python API.

docs.title: Installation and health check
docs.text:
# Download the managed engine binary for the current platform
# (CORE 0.15.0, the version Fleet is tested with)
uv run fleet install-engine

# Verify engine and supporting dependencies
uv run fleet doctor

fleet doctor outputs a structured status report covering: engine binary presence, engine version, pyreadstat availability for XPT serialisation, and environment variable overrides.

docs.title: Python validation API
docs.text:
from fleet import ValidationService

svc = ValidationService()

# Validate an SDTM domain against SDTMIG 3.4
dm_result = svc.validate_sdtm(dm, domain="DM", version="3.4")
dm_result.print_report()  # console: pass/warn/fail by rule
dm_result.save_html_report("outputs/dm_validation.html")  # archivable HTML

# Validate an ADaM dataset against ADaMIG 1.3
adsl_result = svc.validate_adam(adsl, dataset="ADSL", version="1.3")
assert adsl_result.is_valid

The ValidationResult object exposes .is_valid (bool), .print_report(report_type="summary") (or "full" for expanded details including INFO-level engine noise), and .save_html_report(path) — an HTML page with the dataset status and one table row per error, warning and info finding, suitable for archiving as a validation deliverable. Every cell is HTML-escaped, because messages carry data values and the text of custom rules. fleet validate --report writes the same page for a sweep.

docs.title: Engine discovery order
docs.text:
Fleet resolves the engine path at runtime via a four-tier chain (first match wins):

  1. validation.engine_path in study_config.yaml (committable to VCS for team reuse)
  2. FLEET_RULES_ENGINE environment variable (.env at project root)
  3. Managed install under ~/.fleet/cdisc-rules-engine/core/
  4. Legacy ../cdisc-rules-engine/core.py (development fallback)

The study config comes first, so a stale environment variable on one machine cannot replace the engine the team pinned. An explicit rules_engine_path= on .validate() beats all four.

docs.title: Pillar 4 — Automated Test Suite and Static Analysis
docs.text:
Fleet maintains a comprehensive automated test suite executed on every change:

uv run pytest                  # unit + integration tests
uv run ruff check              # style and lint (PEP 8, import ordering, type hints)
uv run ruff format --check     # formatting consistency

In addition, the eight example scripts in examples/ that CI runs are treated as integration smoke tests and must execute without error after every feature change:

uv run python examples/full_pipeline_example.py
uv run python examples/cdiscpilot01_inline.py
uv run python examples/cdiscpilot01_spec_driven.py
uv run python examples/adnca_example.py
uv run python examples/tdd_example.py

These scripts exercise the complete derivation pipeline end-to-end — from raw CSV ingestion through SDTM and ADaM derivation to final export — against the CDISCPILOT01 reference study.

docs.title: Pillar 5 — Local Rule Snapshot (fleet init rules)
docs.text:
Fleet's fleet init rules command caches the exact CDISC conformance rules for the IG versions declared in the study's define.yaml files. Rules are fetched from the CDISC Library API, grouped by domain, and written as human-readable YAML into metadata/sdtm/rules/ and metadata/adam/rules/.

# After fleet init define has created define.yaml files:
uv run fleet init rules

Each YAML file records the rule's CORE ID, description, check logic, scope, and regulatory citations. The files are a reference copy. Validation does not read them: the CORE engine runs the rules bundled in its own release, so the engine version fixes the rules that a study is validated against. Pin the engine with fleet install-engine --version <tag> or with validation.engine_path in study_config.yaml. When committed to VCS, the files provide:

  • Reference: Reviewers can read the rule text for the IG version without re-querying the CDISC Library.
  • Diff visibility: Any change in the CDISC Library rule text between study milestones is visible in version control history.

docs.title: Custom rules
docs.text:
When the standard CDISC CORE rule set does not cover a study-specific requirement, sponsors can author custom rules in the same YAML schema used by the engine.

Fleet provides first-class support for custom rules through:

  • validation.custom_rules in study_config.yaml — sets a team-wide default directory
  • fleet add-rule — scaffolds a schema-valid YAML skeleton with a # TODO Check: block
  • fleet check-rule — validates a rule file (YAML syntax, structure, full JSON Schema)
  • custom_rules= parameter on .validate() — loads rules per-pipeline
# Scaffold a new rule (auto-increments ID)
uv run fleet add-rule --domain AE --description "AESEV required when AESER = Y"

# Validate the rule file before running against datasets
uv run fleet check-rule metadata/custom_rules/FLEET-AE-001.yaml

# Use in pipeline
# .validate("AE", custom_rules="metadata/custom_rules")

Use a company prefix (e.g. ACME-AE-001) to avoid collisions with CORE-XXXXXX.

docs.title: 4. Risk Assessment
docs.text:
Applying the R Validation Hub risk-based framework to Fleet:

Dimension Fleet's profile Risk Intended use Generates submission-ready SDTM/ADaM datasets included in regulatory packages High intended-use criticality Consequence of inaccuracy Incorrect derivations could affect safety/efficacy conclusions; however, CORE validation provides an independent runtime check before submission Mitigated by Pillar 3 Testability 2,900+ unit tests; 39 parity tests with frozen admiral values and a weekly admiral oracle job; CORE conformance checking; example scripts in CI; ruff static analysis High testability → lowers residual risk Open source provenance Public GitHub repository; MIT license; full source inspectable by sponsor QA Transparent Dependency surface Polars ≥ 1.41 (< 2), Pydantic ≥ 2.0, PyYAML ≥ 6.0, httpx ≥ 0.27 (< 1), jsonschema ≥ 4.26, lxml ≥ 6.1. Advisory scan on 5 Nov 2026 with pip-audit over uv export --frozen --no-dev (scope: the lock file without the optional extras): 4 packages with known advisories (anyio, certifi, idna, lxml). On 6 Nov 2026 the lock file took the fixed releases (anyio 4.16.0, certifi 2026.10.23, idna 3.20, lxml 6.1.3), and the same scan found no known advisory. The optional extras are outside this scope and some of their packages have known advisories: scan the set that you install. Repeat the scan at installation; see the dependency statement below Low for the core set at the scan date; scan the extras that you install

Overall risk classification: Medium (high criticality, but substantially mitigated by the five pillars above). Each sponsor assigns its own risk tier in its qualification.

docs.title: Dependency statement
docs.text:
The exact dependency set is the lock file uv.lock. Two commands give it as files for a QA record:

uv export --frozen --no-dev --no-hashes > requirements.txt   # pinned versions
uv export --frozen --no-dev --format cyclonedx1.5 --preview > sbom.json   # CycloneDX SBOM

The CycloneDX export is a uv preview feature and has no licence fields. So the licence summary is written by hand, with its date: Fleet is MIT; on 5 Nov 2026 its direct runtime dependencies were MIT (Polars, Pydantic, PyYAML, jsonschema), BSD-3-Clause (httpx) and BSD-3-Clause (lxml). Check the transitive licences in the SBOM against your policy.

docs.text:
[^1]: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2015). Statistical Software Clarifying Statement. Office of Translational Sciences, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. Available from: https://www.fda.gov/media/161196/download

[^2]: R Validation Hub (2020). A Risk-based Approach for Assessing R Package Accuracy within a Validated Infrastructure. pharmaR Working Group. Available from: https://www.pharmar.org/white-paper/

[^3]: CDISC (2024). CDISC Library API. Available from: https://library.cdisc.org/api

[^4]: Roche, GSK and the pharmaverse community (2021–present). {admiral}: ADaM in R Asset Library. CRAN. Available from: https://cran.r-project.org/package=admiral

[^5]: CDISC (2022–present). CDISC Rules Engine (CORE). Open-source reference implementation for CDISC conformance checking. Available from: https://github.com/cdisc-org/cdisc-rules-engine

docs.title: Why Fleet?
docs.text:
Fleet is designed to bridge the gap between modern, high-performance data engineering and the specialized business logic of clinical statistical programming (SDTM and ADaM).

While traditional tools (like SAS or SQL) or general-purpose Python libraries (like Pandas or plain Polars) are capable of building clinical datasets, they often require writing hundreds of lines of boilerplate code to handle common CDISC requirements: merging controlled terminology, calculating study days, deriving baselines, and maintaining traceability.

Fleet solves this by extending Polars with chainable, domain-specific verbs.

The organising principle is workflow quality: one obvious path from raw data to submission artefact. Everything below — including how well Fleet works with AI coding assistants — falls out of that.

docs.title: 1. Simplicity: Intent-Driven Syntax
docs.text:
With Fleet, your code reads like a specification. Instead of writing complex join logic and conditional expressions, you use verbs that exactly match CDISC concepts.

Without Fleet (Manual Polars):

import polars as pl

# Deriving a baseline value requires multiple steps and intermediate variables
# 1. Filter to baseline records
baseline_df = adbd.filter(pl.col("ABLFL") == "Y").select(["USUBJID", "PARAMCD", "AVAL"])
baseline_df = baseline_df.rename({"AVAL": "BASE"})

# 2. Join back to the main dataset
adbd = adbd.join(baseline_df, on=["USUBJID", "PARAMCD"], how="left")

# 3. Calculate change from baseline
adbd = adbd.with_columns((pl.col("AVAL") - pl.col("BASE")).alias("CHG"))

With Fleet:

import fleet

# Intent is immediately clear in a single chain
adbd = (
    adbd.adam.baseline("BASE", aval="AVAL", baseline_flag="ABLFL", by=["USUBJID", "PARAMCD"])
    .chg("CHG", aval="AVAL", base="BASE")
    .to_frame()
)

docs.title: 2. Power: High Performance Lazy Evaluation
docs.text:
Fleet doesn't just wrap Polars; it deeply integrates with its lazy evaluation engine. When you chain Fleet verbs (e.g., .assign(), .study_day()), most accumulate business logic into a single optimized set of Polars expressions rather than computing immediately.

When you call .to_frame(), Polars executes the plan, with multithreading and query optimization. Most verbs append to one lazy plan. Some verbs read data before the chain continues: checks (baseline, date to a DTC variable) and verbs that build or filter records (whereclauses, pick, derive_*, nodup). The chain does not break at these verbs, so flag → baseline → chg stays one pipeline. The laziness table in the guide lists every verb that reads data. The namespaces are also registered on pl.LazyFrame, so pl.scan_parquet(...).sdtm starts a lazy plan.

  • Native expressions: most Fleet verbs compile down to native Polars pl.Expr objects.
  • Multithreaded: Polars runs the plan on all CPU cores.

docs.title: 3. Clarity: Specification-Driven Development
docs.text:
Fleet natively understands the define.yaml specification. You can define your metadata, controlled terminology, and derivation rules in a single, human-readable file.

Fleet can read this YAML to automatically apply derivations, validate data, and generate CDISC-compliant define.xml exports, ensuring your documentation and your code are never out of sync. A spec entry and an inline call are the same step written two ways — algorithm: chg with aval: AVAL and base: BASE is .chg("CHG", aval="AVAL", base="BASE") — so you can be fully code-driven, fully spec-driven, or a hybrid, and move a step between the two without re-deriving it.

docs.title: 4. Flexibility: Built for Extension
docs.text:
Fleet comes with built-in namespaces for core SDTM (df.sdtm), ADaM BDS (df.adam), ADSL (df.adam.adsl), OCCDS (df.adam.occds), and specialized therapeutic areas (Oncology, Ophthalmology, Vaccines, etc.). Fleet also includes verbs for Body Surface Area (bsa), Mean Arterial Pressure (map), corrected QT (qtc), LOCF imputation, summary record derivation, and parameter-level record generation.

If you have proprietary study requirements, Fleet is designed to be easily extended with custom verbs using standard Polars expressions via the .derivation() method, or by subclassing the namespaces to add your own company-specific logic.

docs.title: 5. Predictability: AI-Native by Consequence
docs.text:
Workflow quality is a promise to human reviewers first. For the same reasons, it is why Fleet works well with AI coding agents.

Coding assistants fail in the same places human newcomers fail. Point one at a codebase with a weak, ambiguous workflow — three ways to derive a baseline, macro names that don't say what they compute, errors that surface three steps later — and it produces plausible code with the wrong derivation. Point the same model at a codebase where the workflow is unambiguous and the search space collapses: the structure itself guides the agent toward the expected outcome, which is what actually raises the probability of a correct first pass.

So Fleet is AI-native by consequence, not by bolt-on. Every property below started as a workflow decision:

  • Standardised Foundation: Built entirely on Python and Polars, two of the most widely represented tools in LLM training data — chosen because they are the ones your team already reads, not to please a model.
  • Unified Package: No need to juggle 10 different sub-packages. One import (import fleet) means there is one place to look, for a person and for an agent.
  • Clear Intent-Driven API: Because derivations are simple verbs (.study_day(), .baseline()), there is usually exactly one right way to express a step. That is what removes the guesswork — and with it, the hallucinations.
  • Tight Feedback Loops: The define.yaml structure is validated through bundled JSON schemas, and CDISC core data validations output structured error arrays. Fast, specific, machine-readable failures let a programmer or an agent course-correct immediately instead of compounding a wrong assumption.
  • Readable Specs: The declarative, YAML-based approach reflects clinical data specification standards, so the artefact a reviewer signs off on and the artefact a model reads are the same file.
  • Built-in llms.txt: Fleet ships structured context (llms.txt, JSON schemas, an MCP server, a define.yaml language server) so the workflow is legible to tooling, not just to people.

docs.title: 6. Native CDISC Library Integration
docs.text:
Fleet has built-in CDISC Library API support. Instead of manually downloading PDF terminology files or maintaining hand-curated codelist dictionaries, Fleet connects directly to the authoritative source.

# Full bootstrapping pipeline: config → define.yaml → codelists.py
fleet init cfg --study-id STUDY01 --domains DM,AE,VS,EX --adam-datasets ADSL,ADVS
fleet init define
fleet init ct

# Or standalone: bootstrap codelists directly from the SDTM IG
fleet add-ct --domains DM,AE,VS,EX --output codelists.py
  • Source of truth is the CDISC Library IG — Fleet queries the Implementation Guide model to discover every variable and codelist for your domains. No manual curation, no guessing concept IDs.
  • IDE auto-completion for CT values — the generated codelists.py gives you typed constants (SEX.M, RACE.WHITE) with full definitions as code comments. Your IDE autocompletes both the codelist name and every permitted submission value.
  • Incremental domain expansion — start with DM and AE, then fleet add-ct --domains LB,CM later. Existing codelists are preserved; only new ones are added.
  • Version-pinned reproducibility — pin your CT package version (e.g. --package sdtmct-2025-09-26) so every team member and CI run generates identical constants.
from codelists import SEX, RACE

dm = (
    raw_df.sdtm.assign("SEX", source="sex", ct=SEX)
    .assign("RACE", source="race", ct=RACE)
    .to_frame()
)

No NCI codes to memorise. No CSV lookups at runtime. Just import the codelist and use it — the _concept_id is carried through for Define-XML generation.

docs.title: Protocol adapters consume a narrow introspection surface, not the registries
docs.text:
The language server reached directly into fleet.core.spec_registry, fleet.core.algorithm_resolver, fleet.define_xml.schema_builder and fleet._version — four private-ish import paths with no contract. Once the VS Code client ships from its own repository on its own cadence, those imports become an accidental public API that no test guards and no version promise covers.

So fleet.introspect is the single contract: algorithms, get_algorithm, suggest_algorithm, algorithm_doc, define_schema, returning purpose-built frozen dataclasses (AlgorithmInfo, ParamInfo, AlgorithmDoc) rather than SpecAlgorithm itself, whose dispatch callable, overwrite_guard and define_template are execution internals that must stay free to change.

Later additions: load_spec_yaml and the Standard type. Since ADR-0008 an algorithm is the verb name, with no aliases.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Additive-only within a major version, tracked by fleet.__version__ alone — no separate surface version. Names, return fields and algorithms may be added; nothing is removed or renamed except on a major. A client therefore declares a minimum Fleet version and never a maximum.
  • The LSP handshake carries the same promise. initialize announces serverInfo of {"name": "fleet-lsp", "version": fleet.__version__}, and a shipped client reads it to enforce that minimum, so it is part of the surface rather than an incidental argument to LanguageServer(...). Pinned by a test alongside the import sweep.
  • The DTOs duplicate part of the registry's shape. That duplication is the price of letting spec_registry be refactored without breaking a shipped extension.
  • An AST sweep in tests/unit/test_introspect.py fails when lsp_server.py imports anything from fleet outside the surface, using the grandfathered-allowlist pattern already established by tests/unit/test_api_conventions.py.
  • mcp_server.py got a weaker boundary, deliberately (#68). It ships inside Fleet and versions with it, so it needs no frozen DTOs and no additive-only promise — nothing external imports it. What it does need is the right dependency direction: it may use Fleet's public packages (fleet, fleet.tlg, fleet.validation, …) and may not import fleet.cli or any private name. tests/unit/test_mcp_boundary.py enforces exactly that.

docs.title: The comparison engine is Fleet's own, written in pure Polars
docs.text: Fleet needs a PROC COMPARE equivalent: pair two datasets on keys, report common and missing variables and observations, list every differing value with tolerances, and give a pass or fail. Polars itself only offers DataFrame.equals and the unit-test assert in polars.testing, and upstream issue pola-rs/polars#14373 has been accepted but unimplemented since February 2024. We decided to write the engine ourselves as Polars expressions in a dedicated comparison package, with the CLI verb, the top-level fleet.compare function and the namespace verb as thin callers over it, and to take no new runtime dependency.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• datacompy (Capital One) accepts Polars input but hard-requires pandas and numpy, runs its numeric comparison through np.isclose, and pins polars below the current release. Adopting it would put pandas back into Fleet's core dependency set and tie our polars upgrades to theirs.
  • diffly (QuantCo) is pure Polars and actively maintained, but it requires a primary key, has no BY groups, no variable pairing and no pass/fail code in the SAS sense, and brings rich with it. The SAS-shaped layer we need is most of the work, so wrapping it saves little and leaves a small third-party package on the QC-critical path that Fleet's qualification strategy would then have to cover.
  • Contributing upstream to Polars is the right long-term home, but two and a half years of open API debate rule it out of Fleet's critical path.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The comparison engine is qualified as Fleet code, with its own SAS-parity fixtures, rather than as an inherited dependency.
  • Fleet keeps its promise of a pure-Polars core: pandas and numpy stay confined to the optional io extra. Amended by ADR-0010: the io extra now reads and writes SAS files through the Polars route of pyreadstat, with no pandas.
  • If Polars ships a native compare later, fleet.compare can delegate to it behind the same three surfaces without changing the comparison report.

docs.title: One run setup for every validation surface
docs.text: The verb .validate(), fleet validate, the MCP tool fleet_validate and the fleet check gate each resolved the standard, the IG version, the custom rules and the engine in their own way, so one study gave different rules on different surfaces. We decided that one module in fleet.validation builds a run setup, a fixed record of every input of a validation with the source of each, and that every surface validates from it and resolves nothing itself.

docs.title: Decisions a reader would not expect
docs.text:
• The study config beats FLEET_RULES_ENGINE inside a study. The usual order lets the environment override a config file. We reversed it because a team lead pins validation.engine_path so that every programmer runs the same rule build; a stale environment variable on one machine would silently give different QC findings. The environment variable still applies outside a study, and every report prints the engine path and version it used.
  • Official and custom rules run in two engine runs. CORE 0.15.0 treats -lr as a replacement for its rule set, not an addition: one AE file ran 430 official rules without -lr and 2 local rules with it. One run would drop every CDISC rule as soon as a study sets validation.custom_rules. The two results join into one report and each finding names its source.
  • A sweep is one engine run per standard, because the engine takes one standard per run. SDTM and ADaM results still join into one report and one exit code.
  • The IG version list is fixed in Fleet, not read from core list-rule-sets, so that fleet check gives the same answer in CI, where no engine is installed, as on a programmer's machine.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep resolution on each surface and share helpers. Rejected: the drift came from four call sites choosing which helpers to call, and helpers do not stop a fifth surface from skipping one.
  • Let the environment variable win, as today. Rejected for the reason above.
  • Keep the engine's -lr behaviour and warn that official rules did not run. Rejected: one line in a long report is easy to miss at delivery.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A study with custom rules takes about twice as long to validate.
  • A new CORE release that adds an IG version needs a Fleet release before Fleet accepts it.
  • A setup problem (unclear standard, unsupported IG version) is its own outcome, "could not run": exit 2 on the CLI, an exception on the verb, and an outcome field on the MCP tool.

docs.title: A compare that checks no values keeps the two-value verdict and warns
docs.text: When the two sides share only their keys, or both have no observations, a compare checks no values. Before this decision, fleet.compare and the .compare() verb returned a verdict, but fleet compare exited 2 ("could not run"), because the CLI held its own check. ADR-0002 makes the CLI, the function and the verb thin callers over one engine, so we decided that the engine alone gives the verdict and the callers only translate it. The verdict keeps its two values, EQUAL and NOT EQUAL. A key-only compare follows the observations: the same key values on both sides are EQUAL, and a one-sided key or variable is NOT EQUAL. Two empty sides are EQUAL. In both cases the report warns that no values were checked. The warning does not change the verdict and does not trigger on_fail. A variables= restriction that names only keys is an argument mistake, so the engine refuses it with ComparisonError.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Raise ComparisonError whenever nothing is compared. This breaks a subject-list check (USUBJID only on both sides), and it hides the variables summary that shows why nothing matched. PROC COMPARE lists the common and the one-sided variables in this case, and does not stop.
  • A third verdict, NOT COMPARABLE. Every caller, on_fail, the JSON consumers and the VS Code extension would need to learn a third state, and is_equal would no longer answer the whole question.
  • A new flag, for example no_observations. An empty domain early in a study (ADAE with no AEs yet) would fail on every rerun. Programmers would learn to ignore the flag, and that hides the real flags next to it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• fleet compare now exits 1, and prints the full report, when the sides share only keys but carry other variables. Before, it exited 2 with a message on stderr only.
  • A script that checks only the verdict or the exit code passes a key-only or an empty compare. The warning is the only signal, so a QC reviewer reads it.

docs.title: Summary specs are the engine contract
docs.text: Every summary table in fleet.tlg goes through one engine, summarize_ard, and before this decision 21 namespace methods restated its contract by forwarding 13 to 16 keyword arguments each, in 8 different shapes, with two template rules hidden in method bodies: the fill of uncoded terms and the exclusion of the baseline record. We decided that the summary spec is the engine contract. A seam function, summarize_spec(df, spec, *, groupby, adsl), resolves the group column, validates the frame, prepares it from the spec, and calls the engine from the spec's fields. The two hidden rules become spec fields, uncoded and prefilter, with a default per template, visible in the YAML and settable through the builder. The cards context string and the nested flag are class attributes of the spec class, not YAML fields, because one spec class serves exactly one template method.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Route every method through the seam, composites included. Seven methods do real work between the filter and the engine: the deaths table calls the engine twice on different populations, the shift table builds its own worst-case frame, the demographics table adds a continuous block, and the AE severity, grade and relationship tables reduce to the worst record per subject before counting. Pushing that logic into a spec hides an algorithm in data. These seven keep the keyword engine and share only the preparation step.
  • Keep the uncoded fill and the baseline guard as template facts in code. An SAP can specify the uncoded label and whether baseline is excluded. A spec that cannot say so is not a spec of the table.
  • Typed switches instead of a prefilter expression. exclude_baseline: true reads well, but every new template would add a boolean to the shared base, and a QC programmer still could not see the exact rule. The expression uses the same whitelisted parser as dataset_filter and the SDTM specs.
  • Concentrate every spec class in the shared specs module. The review's deletion test pointed there. With the domain modules kept as the typed public surface, a domain's spec next to its three-line method is the smaller file to open, so the shared module keeps only the base classes and the building blocks.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every column a prefilter names is a required column of the template. A change-from-baseline table on an ADLB or ADEG without ABLFL, and an exposure table on an ADEX without PARCAT1, now refuse to run. Before, the guard was skipped without a message and baseline or per-period records were counted. prefilter: null in the spec is the visible escape hatch.
  • The order of the preparation step is fixed: uncoded fill, then dataset filter, then prefilter. A dataset filter may therefore reference the uncoded label.
  • A composite applies the dataset filter before its own reduction. On the lab shift table the filter used to run after the worst-case reduction, so a filtered-out record could decide a subject's worst range indicator; it no longer can.
  • Every column a prefilter names is required through prefilter_columns(), read from the expression at validation time, not through the static required_columns list. Setting prefilter=None lifts the requirement with the rule.
  • A user-registered template keeps its signature, fn(df, *, adsl, spec, groupby), and may call the seam or the engine.

docs.title: A study run carries only derivation-free columns from its inputs, and pins every input
docs.text: fleet run left-joined every column a dataset declares from its extra inputs on USUBJID, and pinned nothing, so a define that uses merge, lookup, first_date, last_date or count_events ran from Python and failed from the CLI (#86). We decided that a study run pins every input under its dataset name, and that the implicit join brings only the carry-through columns: the declared variables that have no derivation. A variable with a derivation comes from its algorithm alone.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep the join of every declared column, and pin as well. Rejected: a variable declared with lookup from ADSL would arrive twice, and the overwrite guard in from_spec would stop the run on the second arrival.
  • No implicit join, pins only. Rejected: every carried column would need a derivation line. The pilot study alone has 41 such columns across ADVS, ADAE and ADEX, and the Define-XML would gain 41 methods that say "copied".

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• "No derivation" has one meaning in a define: carried from an input, unchanged. The glossary entry is "carry-through column".
  • A define that declares a column with no derivation and expects Python code to compute it later gets the input's value instead. The column must be left out of the define or given a derivation.
  • The join on USUBJID runs only when a step has carry-through columns to bring, so a step with none needs no USUBJID.

docs.title: Spec parameter facts come from the verb signature, and the spec may be stricter than the verb but never looser
docs.text:
Status: superseded by ADR-0008 on 2026-10-16. The verb is the algorithm, so the Param tables and the five rules below go with the implementation of ADR-0008. The consequence that survives: the spec is never looser than the verb, and a define.yaml names its inputs.

Every spec algorithm in fleet.core.spec_registry restated its verb's parameters in a hand-written Param table: the name, the type, the default, and whether the field is required. The parity test checked that the algorithm names and the JSON schema matched the registry, but it never compared the parameter tables with the verb signatures. A renamed keyword or a changed default on the verb passed green, and the inline form and the define.yaml form of one derivation then produced different numbers. On 2026-10-14 we measured the two sides: 48 algorithms, 24 of them with a Param table equal to the signature, 73 individual differences on the other 24. Most of the differences were deliberate, so "the signature is the declaration" was not true of the registry as it stood, and we had to decide what the registry is allowed to say that the signature does not.

We decided that the registry keeps two vocabularies (the spec algorithm names a data-standards reviewer reads, assign_ct, hardcode_no_ct, mapped onto one verb per intent) and that within one algorithm the spec fields take their default and required facts from the verb signature. A Param declares only what a signature cannot say: the spec field name when it differs from the keyword (kwarg), the YAML type (annotation), a legacy alias, a dispatch-time conversion (convert), whether the target name is the default (default_to_target), and required=True where the spec is stricter than the verb. The registry reads the signature on first lookup, not at import, so spec_registry never imports the namespace classes at module load. The description falls back to the Args: line of the verb docstring when the Param does not state one.

The rule the parity test enforces, for every algorithm with default dispatch and every Param:

  1. The keyword exists in the verb signature.
  2. A Param marked default-to-target skips the default check.
  3. The spec may be stricter than the verb: required=True where the signature has a default. The spec may never be looser: no spec-only default where the signature requires a value, and no spec-only default that differs from the signature's.
  4. When both sides are optional, the defaults are equal.
  5. Verb arguments absent from the registry are ignored. The spec surface is a curated subset of the signature, widened when a Define-XML method template exists for the new field.

Custom-dispatch algorithms (date, nsv, callable, pick) have no verb signature to derive from and are outside the rule.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• The verb is the algorithm (#146). One name, one declaration, one record: the algorithm: value is the verb name and the YAML keys are its keyword arguments, so the Param tables disappear. This reverses the recorded choice "Two vocabularies, one mapping" in docs/concepts/define-yaml.md, changes the vocabulary a reviewer reads in a define.yaml, and cannot make ct_codelist required for a CT assignment while leaving it absent for a plain copy, because one signature cannot produce five strict models. It stays open as its own decision. If it is taken, it deletes the Param tables and this ADR with them.
  • Keep spec-only defaults as CDISC conventions. nrind in YAML defaulted low to LBSTNRLO while the Python call required low=; merge and lookup in YAML defaulted on to USUBJID while the Python verb raises without it. A submission artefact should name its inputs, and a merge that silently joins on USUBJID when the author meant USUBJID and VISITNUM duplicates rows with no trace in the spec. All ten spec-only defaults go, and the keys become required in YAML. No shipped example, doc or test spec omitted any of them.
  • Derive the YAML type from the Python type. The two type systems differ on purpose: ct is str | type | None in Python and a codelist id in YAML, agg is a list of Polars expressions in Python and a list of strings in YAML. The convert field exists because of that gap. The annotation is a declaration, not a restatement, so it stays written.
  • A test only, no derivation. The classified parity test closes the live bug on its own. Derivation is what makes drift impossible instead of tested-for, and it turns each of the 48 registrations planned in #90 into one Param per field plus a method template. The test lands first, then derivation.
  • Resolve at import through a finalize() call in fleet/__init__, or a hook on namespace class creation. Both make the import order of fleet/__init__ a hidden contract, or couple the registry to the namespace mixin. Resolution on first lookup follows fleet.introspect.algorithms(), which refuses to cache for the same reason.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• ct_codelist becomes required on assign_ct and hardcode_ct. The concept doc already claimed that a CT derivation missing its codelist is a load-time error, and the registry now makes that true.
  • A define.yaml must state low, high and aval for nrind, the three dates for on_treatment, term_var for atoxgr, and on for merge and lookup. A missing key is a load-time error with a suggestion.
  • A misspelled keyword in a registration surfaces at first lookup, not at import. The parity test touches every entry, so it is still a red test.
  • The review's count "5 of Param's 10 fields become derived" is corrected to 2: default and required. description has a fallback, not a derivation.
  • fleet.introspect.ParamInfo does not change. A default field may be added later under ADR-0001's additive rule.
  • SpecAlgorithm.verb stays the attribute name on the standard's top-level namespace. Sub-namespace verbs need a dotted path, which is #90's design.

docs.title: The verb is the algorithm: one vocabulary for inline code and define.yaml
docs.text:
Status: accepted, 2026-10-16. Proposed and decided the same day in #146. Supersedes ADR-0007. Implemented on 2026-10-17 on branch feat/146-verb-is-the-algorithm.

A derivation has two notations in Fleet. The inline notation is a verb call, .assign("SEX", source="sex", ct=SEX). The spec notation is a derivation: block in a define.yaml, algorithm: assign_ct, source: sex, ct_codelist: C66731. Today the two notations use two vocabularies. The spec registry maps the spec names onto the verbs with a hand-written Param table per algorithm, and ADR-0007 made the table take its default and required facts from the verb signature. The table still exists, and so do the renamed keys, the aliases and the legacy keys.

We decided that the algorithm: value is the verb name and the YAML keys are the keyword arguments of the verb. The rule for the programmer: remove .verb("TARGET", and the last ). What stays is the YAML block. Fleet builds the strict Pydantic model from the verb signature. A short declaration per verb says only what a signature cannot say: which arguments stay out of the spec, which arguments exclude each other, and the Define-XML method text. Lineage already records (verb, target, kwargs). from_spec calls the verb with them, and to_spec_yaml() writes them back unchanged.

docs.title: Measured on 2026-10-16, on main at bb4b878
docs.text:
Fact Value Registered algorithms 46 (16 SDTM, 30 ADaM) Distinct verbs behind them 39 (13 SDTM, 26 ADaM) Verbs with more than one spec name assign (4 names in SDTM, 3 in ADaM), derivation (2), duration (2) Spec names that differ from their only verb if_then_else, condderivation (case_when), lookup (merge), callable (derivation) Renamed keys 13 distinct renames on 22 fields, for example ct_codelist for ct, groups for by, else_value for else_ Algorithm aliases 4: assign_dtc, dataset_level, count, mean_arterial_pressure Legacy key maps 8 Custom dispatch 4: date (SDTM), nsv, pick, callable Registration code in spec_registry.py 894 lines (lines 857 to 1751) Shipped define.yaml files with derivations 4 files, 174 blocks Blocks whose algorithm: value changes 160 of 174 Blocks where a key changes 18 of 174

The 160 name changes are mostly source and assign_no_ct to assign (108 blocks) and assign_dtc to date (14 blocks).

docs.title: Before and after
docs.text:
The DM block for SEX, today and under this proposal. The inline call is .assign("SEX", source="sex", ct=SEX, ct_map={"F": "F", "M": "M"}).

# today
- name: SEX
  codelist: C66731
  derivation:
    algorithm: assign_ct
    source: sex
    ct_codelist: C66731
    ct_mapping: { "F": "F", "M": "M" }

# proposed
- name: SEX
  codelist: C66731
  derivation:
    algorithm: assign
    source: sex
    ct_map: { "F": "F", "M": "M" }

ct: is absent in the proposed block. It defaults to the codelist: of the variable. More examples:

Inline call Spec block today Spec block proposed .assign("DOMAIN", value="DM") algorithm: hardcode_no_ct, value: DM algorithm: assign, value: DM .case_when("ARMCD", when=[...], else_="X") algorithm: if_then_else, when:, else_value: X algorithm: case_when, when:, else: X .duration("ADY", start="TRTSDT", end="ASTDT") algorithm: study_day, reference_date:, analysis_date: algorithm: duration, start:, end: .seq("AESEQ", by=["USUBJID"]) algorithm: seq, groups: [USUBJID] algorithm: seq, by: [USUBJID] .merge(dataset=adsl, on=["USUBJID"]) algorithm: lookup, dataset: ADSL, on: algorithm: merge, dataset: ADSL, on: .onco.best_overall_response("BOR", ...) none (#90) algorithm: onco.best_overall_response

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
1. One name. The algorithm: value is the verb name. Sub-namespace verbs use a dotted name, pk.blq_flag. No aliases, no legacy keys.
  2. One declaration. The verb signature is the spec schema. Every keyword argument of the verb is a YAML key, except the arguments the verb declaration excludes. required and default come from the signature, as in ADR-0007.
  3. One type table. The YAML type comes from the Python type through a fixed table. A pl.Expr is an expression string. A pl.DataFrame | pl.LazyFrame is the name of a pinned dataset. A codelist class (str | type) is a codelist id. A @derivation object is its registered name or dotted path. Every other type is written as is.
  4. One trailing underscore. A keyword that ends in _ because it shadows a Python word loses the underscore in YAML. else_ is else:.
  5. One record. The lineage node's verb and kwargs are the block. derivation_from_lineage has one candidate, not a ranked list. The static converter (#139) is the same mapping on literal arguments.

The declaration per verb is short. A sketch:

spec_verb(
    "assign",
    standard="sdtm",
    exclude=("ct_validator", "validate_values"),
    one_of=("source", "value"),
    method_text=[
        ({"value", "ct"}, "Set to the controlled terminology value '{value}' for all records."),
        ({"value"}, "Set to '{value}' for all records."),
        ({"source", "ct"}, "Value of {source} mapped to controlled terminology."),
        ({"source"}, "Direct copy of {source}."),
    ],
)

The method_text list is where the reviewer vocabulary survives. The Define-XML MethodDef still reads "Value of SEX mapped to controlled terminology", chosen by the keys the block gives. The reviewer reads the Define-XML. The YAML names move to the programmer's vocabulary.

docs.title: What one signature cannot say, and the answer
docs.text:
• assign needs exactly one of source and value. A one_of group on the declaration, enforced by a model validator. A block with both, or neither, is a load-time error.
  • A CT copy without its codelist. Today assign_ct requires ct_codelist, and assign_no_ct has none. Under one verb ct is optional. The proposal moves the strictness to the variable: ct: defaults to the variable's codelist:, and a ct_map on a variable without codelist: and without ct: is a load-time error, because a mapping needs a codelist. This also closes the drift between ct_codelist and codelist: that #96 reports.
  • Copy-through where the source is the target. source keeps its default-to-target behaviour. It is one flag on the declaration, as today.
  • study_day in YAML runs duration today. Under the rule study_day names the pin-based study_day verb, which is inline-only. The migration rewrites the three shipped study_day blocks to duration.
  • Four verbs whose call shape is not a flat kwargs dict. date (SDTM), nsv, pick and the callable form of derivation keep a custom dispatch. callable: stays the YAML key for a @derivation object, under algorithm: derivation, and the shorthand callable: alone still injects the algorithm.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep two vocabularies (ADR-0007, the status quo). The spec reads assign_ct where a data-standards reviewer expects it. The cost is the 894-line table, the five parity rules that guard it, 13 renamed keys to learn, and every new verb paid twice: #90 plans 48 more Param tables. The static converter must rank candidates for one verb, and to_spec_yaml() relabels lineage nodes to the spec name. Rejected: the inline verbs and the spec-driven derivations must match, and the reviewer reads the Define-XML, where the method text keeps the standards vocabulary.
  • Rename the verbs to the spec names. .assign_ct(...), .hardcode_no_ct(...), .if_then_else(...) as inline verbs. One vocabulary, but four verbs for one intent, and the inline API becomes the define dialect. Rejected.
  • Verb names in YAML, old names kept as aliases for one minor version. The table stays alive to serve the aliases, so nothing is deleted until the next version. Fleet is pre-alpha at 0.2.0a1, #146 states that no compatibility is owed, and fleet migrate already exists for the Python side. Rejected in favour of a hard cut with a spec migration.
  • Rename the key algorithm: to verb:. Honest, but it changes the JSON schema root, the LSP completions, every doc and every shipped spec for a word. The key stays algorithm:.
  • Derive the YAML type from the Python type. ADR-0007 rejected this, because ct and agg differ between Python and YAML on purpose. The proposal keeps that difference, but as a fixed four-row table instead of a per-field annotation and convert. The table is the declaration.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Deleted:

  • The Param tables, annotation, kwarg, alias, convert, legacy_keys and aliases. About 894 lines become an estimated 200 (measured after implementation: 39 declarations in 330 lines, of which 60 are Define-XML text).
  • The five parity rules of ADR-0007 and the kwarg renames. The remaining test is one rule: the YAML model of a verb equals its signature minus the excluded arguments.
  • The SDTMAlgorithm and ADAMAlgorithm enums in fleet.sdtm.models and fleet.adam.models. They are exported from fleet and hold the spec names. They go, or they are generated from the verb list.
  • The rules ALG01 to ALG05 in fleet.define_xml.validator. They check source_variable, constant_value, merge_dataset and merge_key under item_defs, keys the current dialect does not have. No shipped define.yaml uses them.
  • ADR-0007, marked superseded.

Changed:

  • Every shipped define.yaml: 174 blocks in 4 files, plus the YAML in docs/ and the inline dicts in tests/. define_spec_schema.json is regenerated, llms.txt is rebuilt.
  • fleet migrate gains a spec mode. It rewrites a define.yaml with a frozen old-to-new table kept as a data file, so a study moves in one command and the mapping does not depend on the deleted registry.
  • fleet.introspect keeps its DTOs. AlgorithmInfo.name now holds verb names. ADR-0001's additive-only rule covers the names and shapes of the surface, not the catalogue values. The VS Code client reads the catalogue from the LSP at run time; fleet-vscode/src/server.ts hard-codes no algorithm name (checked 2026-10-16).
  • _attach_spec_lineage no longer relabels nodes. The verb on the node is the algorithm.
  • docs/concepts/define-yaml.md replaces "Two vocabularies, one mapping" with the one rule.

Risks:

  • The define.yaml reads like Python. by, ct_map, when. A programmer who knows SAS and CDISC but not Fleet learns the verb vocabulary once, in both notations instead of two.
  • A verb signature change is now a spec dialect change. A renamed keyword breaks every study's define.yaml. The signature becomes a contract: a rename needs a fleet migrate entry and a fleet_spec_version note. ADR-0007 already made a default change a spec change, so this is one step further on the same path.
  • The strict CT check moves from the algorithm name to the variable's codelist:. A variable without codelist: and without ct: gets no CT check, as today for assign_no_ct.

docs.title: Decided on 2026-10-16
docs.text:
The five questions of the proposal and their answers.

  1. Who reads the define.yaml? Domain. The inline verbs and the spec-driven derivations must match. The algorithm: value is the verb name, assign. A QC programmer reads the same name in the program and in the spec.
  2. ct: defaults to the variable's codelist:. Domain. Yes. For DM.SEX with codelist: C66731, a derivation algorithm: assign, source: sex and no ct: checks the raw values against C66731. A ct_map on a variable without codelist: and without ct: is a load-time error.
  3. else_ is written else: in YAML. Engineering. Yes. A trailing underscore that avoids a Python keyword is dropped in YAML.
  4. Hard cut or aliases. Engineering. Hard cut. Fleet is pre-alpha. An old define.yaml fails at load with a message that names fleet migrate --spec.
  5. The key stays algorithm:. Engineering. Yes.

docs.title: Decisions taken without a question
docs.text:
• The ADR number is 0008. ADR-0006 is on PR #175 and may move this number.
  • The four custom-dispatch algorithms stay as they are.
  • Sub-namespace verbs use the dotted verb name. This answers the blocker in #90.
  • The Define-XML method text is chosen per verb by the keys given in the block, in declared order, first match wins.
  • The type table has four rows: expression, pinned dataset, codelist, derivation object.
  • callable: stays as a key under algorithm: derivation, and the shorthand without algorithm: stays.
  • The study_day blocks in YAML migrate to duration.

docs.title: Implementation phases
docs.text:
Each phase is one PR. The next phase starts when the previous one is green.

  1. spec_verb() next to spec_algorithm(). The new declaration registers the 39 verbs under their verb names, with the type table, exclude, one_of and method_text. The old names resolve to the new entries. A new parity test checks that each YAML model equals its signature. from_spec, to_spec_yaml(), the static converter and the schema builder all pass on the old shipped YAML.
  2. Migration. fleet migrate --spec with the frozen table. The 4 shipped specs, the docs YAML, the tests and define_spec_schema.json move to the verb names. The six examples pass.
  3. Deletion. spec_algorithm, Param, the aliases, the legacy keys, the enums, the ALG rules, the five ADR-0007 rules and _attach_spec_lineage go. ADR-0007 is marked superseded. define-yaml.md and llms.txt are rewritten.
  4. Follow-ups. #90 becomes 48 one-line registrations. #89 extends the parity test to the sub-namespaces. #137 and #138 shrink, because the converter is the one mapping.

Verification for every phase: uv run ruff check && uv run ruff format --check, uv run pytest, the six examples, uv run python scripts/build_llms.py --check, and uv run python -m fleet.define_xml.schema_builder with a clean diff.

docs.title: An admission bar for clinical verbs, and verbs() as the discovery seam
docs.text: The architecture review of 30 August 2026 (candidate 3, #160) found two problems on the therapeutic-area surface. No written rule said when a verb earns its place, so metabolic.waist_hip_ratio (one division) sat next to vaccine.seroconversion_flag (a four-fold threshold and a guard against division by zero). And every TA namespace inherits about 41 shared verbs, so autocomplete shows 45 names for the 4 a namespace adds. We decided that a new clinical verb must pass one test, that the test applies forwards only, and that verbs() is the discovery seam, not autocomplete.

docs.title: The decision
docs.text:
• Two kinds of verb. A chain verb supplies a mechanism and encodes no clinical rule (derivation, case_when, merge, pin). A clinical verb encodes a rule a programmer would otherwise copy from a standard or an SAP: a threshold, a constant, a guard, a mapping or an ordering. The terms are in CONTEXT.md.
  • The admission bar. A new clinical verb is added only if this holds: if the verb were deleted, a programmer who rewrites it inline must be able to get a wrong answer, not only type more. A constant typed by hand qualifies, because a typo in 10.8 gives a wrong answer silently. A threshold the caller supplies does not qualify, because the verb is then case_when with a shorter name.
  • The citation is part of the bar. A clinical verb's docstring names the rule it encodes under a References: section: the standard or guidance, the year, and the convention when no standard fixes the value. The citation is what a QC programmer checks against the SAP.
  • The bar applies to every clinical verb, in every namespace. It is about what a verb encodes, not where it lives. It applies to new verbs only.
  • verbs() is the discovery seam. It gains an origin column: the path a programmer types to reach the namespace that defines the verb (sdtm, adam, adam.metabolic), or core for the verbs every namespace shares. Every row stays, so nothing that reads the frame today breaks.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Delete the weak verbs. Rejected: the shared verbs fill the completion list, not the TA verbs, so deleting four names changes 45 completions into 41. The fleet migrate precedent (six spellings of assign became one) stays available if the surface keeps growing.
  • Filter autocomplete. Rejected: Pylance builds completions statically and never calls __dir__, and a TA verb must chain into .derivation() and .to_frame(), so the inherited verbs must stay visible.
  • An inherited=False parameter on verbs(). Rejected: the same call would return a different row count depending on a flag. A column and a plain Polars filter do the same work with no new behaviour.
  • A unit test that fails on a docstring without References:. Deferred: the rule costs nothing in prose, and a fake citation passes a format check anyway. Revisit if the surface keeps growing.
  • Admit a verb when a published standard fixes a constant, with no wrong-answer test. Rejected: it admits every formula the SAP already gives, and the surface grows with verbs that save typing only.

docs.title: Grandfathered verbs
docs.text:
These eight fail the bar today and are kept, because the bar applies forwards only. Nothing depends on their removal.

Verb Why it fails metabolic.waist_hip_ratio One division, one rounding. metabolic.waist_height_ratio One division, one rounding. neuro.cdrsob_total A sum of columns. neuro.panss_total A sum of three columns. peds.age_days One date difference. vaccine.seroresponse_flag The caller supplies the threshold. ophtha.bcva_criterion The caller supplies the threshold and the direction. onco.tumor_response_flag The caller supplies the response list; the default is is_in(["CR", "PR"]).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Writing the references for the 20 TA verbs that pass exposed what the bar is for. vaccine.fever_flag flags strictly above 38.0 °C, while the FDA toxicity grading scale (2007) and the Brighton Collaboration define fever from 38.0 °C. peds.bmi_category applies the WHO adult cut-offs from the pediatrics namespace, where age- and sex-specific percentiles apply. neuro.mmse_category used severity bands (27, 18, 10) that no published scheme fixes; it now defaults to Tombaugh and McIntyre (1992) and takes the cut-offs as arguments, since admiralneuro ships no MMSE rule. The first two are tracked issues, not a change in this decision.
  • A verb whose threshold comes from the SAP rather than a standard can still pass, when the verb adds a guard or an ordering the programmer would get wrong. Its References: then names the convention and says "check the SAP".
  • fleet.introspect is unchanged. verbs() is a namespace method, not part of the introspection surface, and the new column is additive.
  • This ADR was written as 0005 on its branch. It takes 0009, because 0005 to 0008 were taken on main before it merged.

docs.title: SAS files follow SAS rules: a blank is missing, a missing key matches, transport is version 5
docs.text: The alpha audit of 2 November 2026 (package F) found that Fleet read and wrote SAS files by Polars rules, not SAS rules. A blank character value stayed "", so is_null() missed it and seven TLG templates printed rows with no label. Once a blank becomes null, a Polars join drops a null key, where SAS MERGE BY matches missing to missing. The XPT writer made a version 8 file with the member DATASET and stored a date as DATETIME seconds, and both directions needed pandas, which no documented install provides. We decided that every SAS file follows the SAS rule at the reader and the writer, and that every verb join follows SAS MERGE BY.

docs.title: The decision
docs.text:
• A SAS blank reads as null. SAS has one character missing value, the blank, and an XPT file cannot tell a blank from a missing value. The XPT and SAS7BDAT reader turns "" into null, with no opt-out. admiral asks for the same step (convert_blanks_to_na) before any derivation.
  • A missing key matches a missing key. Every verb that joins on keys the user names (merge, pick, first_date, last_date, count_events, merge_adsl, flag with exists, flag_relative, derive_param, the pin joins and the TTE joins) joins with nulls_equal=True. SAS MERGE BY and dplyr do the same, so an admiral port and a SAS double program give the same records.
  • A blank from another tool is a value until the user says otherwise. fleet.compare stays exact: "" against null differs. blank_is_missing=True (--blank-is-missing) reads "" as null on both sides, keys included, and the settings line shows it.
  • XPT goes through the Polars route of pyreadstat, version 5. Read with output_format="polars", write a Polars frame with file_format_version=5. The member is the file name (FDA TCG 3.1.1). A date is SAS days with DATE9, a datetime seconds with DATETIME20, a time seconds with TIME8. NaN and infinity become missing; infinity warns. A name over 8 characters, a label over 40 or a value over 200 bytes stops the write, because a cut value is a silent change.
  • A value that is not ASCII is written as UTF-8 bytes, with a warning. TCG 3.1.5 allows UTF-8 and advises against it, and a stop would block every study that is not for the FDA.
  • A CSV file holds no types; Fleet decides them in the open. load_raw_data infers from every row and keeps a column with a leading zero as text, with a warning. fleet run reads define type text variables, and their raw sources, as text. fleet compare types a CSV side against the other side, or across both CSV sides: text when a value has a leading zero or is not a number, a number otherwise, and --text as the $ informat.
  • The encoding is the user's to name. load_raw_data(..., encoding=) reaches pyreadstat and Polars, and --encoding is on fleet compare and fleet validate. A keyword a reader does not take raises.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• A blank rule in the TLG engine (prepare_frame). Rejected: it cannot reach ADSL or the verbs, so ADSL and the table would disagree. One fix at the reader covers them all.
  • Keep the pandas route and declare pandas and pyarrow in the io extra. Rejected: two heavy dependencies for a conversion the reader does natively, and the pandas route stores a Polars date as DATETIME.
  • Stop the write on a value that is not ASCII. Rejected for the reason above; the warning names the column.
  • "" and null always equal in fleet compare. Rejected: the two frames give different is_null() results, so a production pipeline that skipped the blank step would pass QC and still give a wrong table.
  • All CSV columns as text in fleet compare. Rejected: AVAL 1.10 against 1.1 would differ and --abs-tol would do nothing.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• pyreadstat>=1.3.3 is the floor of the io extra: 1.2.x and 1.3.0 reject a Polars frame. A CI job installs the io extra alone and checks that pandas and pyarrow are absent.
  • DatasetChecker.write_xpt calls save_xpt with the define labels and refuses a file named after another dataset.
  • fleet run --format xpt and fleet tdd build --format xpt write dataset and variable labels from define.yaml and the packaged SDTMIG structures.
  • This amends ADR-0002, which assumed that pandas lives in the io extra.

docs.title: One reader for --DTC text, and the date rules it carries
docs.text: The alpha audit of 2 November 2026 (package A) found 43 places in src/fleet that parsed --DTC text, each in its own way. A time part made study_day null, a partial date won a text minimum in first_date, a slash date was read day first with no message, and select(spec=) turned a partial AESTDTC into null. We decided that every date verb reads --DTC text through one module, fleet.core.dtc, and that the module never guesses.

docs.title: The decision
docs.text:
• One reader. date_part gives the date of a value with a complete, real date; datetime_part the date-time of a value with hours and minutes; is_iso8601 checks the SDTMIG 3.4 forms (right truncation, hyphens for missing components, offsets, intervals). Day arithmetic uses the date portion (SDTMIG 3.4 section 4.4.4). A partial date gives null in a day count (CG0007).
  • Warnings run at collect. warn_on_collect wraps the result, so the plan stays lazy and the message can quote the raw text: one warning per call, with the count and the first five values.
  • .sdtm.date() never guesses. A valid ISO 8601 value stays. YYYYMMDD and DD-MON-YYYY convert, because they cannot be read two ways. A slash date or a two-digit year raises until format= names the layout, as an explicit SAS informat and the required .format of sdtm.oak do (Mahdi, Q4 A). Any other value becomes null with a warning (c1-90 A).
  • A time joins a date by SDTMIG 4.4.2. A blank time leaves the date; a partial date takes one hyphen per missing component; a time with no date gives -----T08:30, as sdtm.oak does (Q5 A).
  • Baseline is strictly before the reference. A record on the reference date is eligible only when both times are known and it is earlier (Q1 B, the IG text "prior to" and sdtm.oak derive_blfl).
  • EPOCH on a transition date with no time follows the record kind. Findings (--DTC) take the earlier element, Events and Interventions (--STDTC) the later one, and epoch_assign(same_day=) overrides (Q2 E). No guidance fixes this case, so the warning gives the rule for the SDRG.
  • Duration adds one day only when the end is on or after the start, before the division for weeks, months and years, and never for hours, minutes and seconds by default (admiral compute_duration; Q3 A).
  • A date-time keeps every collected part. Only missing parts are imputed, by position; a fraction stays; an offset is dropped with a warning, so the wall clock stays (admiral).
  • A bound moves only an imputed date whose possible range holds it; a complete date never moves (admiral derive_vars_dt).
  • First and last dates compare dates. A partial value is left out with a warning unless impute= states the SAP rule, which then writes the *DTF flag of the winning record.
  • select(spec=) never casts --DTC and never imputes. SDTM columns stay text; ADaM *DT and *DTM are read from text, and a value that is not complete becomes null with a warning. DatasetChecker expects text for every *DTC.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep format inference per column. Rejected: the result of one row depended on the other rows, and a column of timed values raised.
  • Warn and keep a guess for slash dates. Rejected: the wrong date reaches AESTDTC and TRTEMFL, and one warning in a long log is easy to miss.
  • Collect a snapshot at each verb for the warnings. Rejected: it runs the plan twice. The check inside the plan sees the same raw text.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Date-only data changes in one place: a record on the reference date is no longer baseline unless both times show it is earlier.
  • first_date and last_date on --DTC text now give pl.Date (or pl.Datetime for *DTM), not text.
  • epoch_assign with same_day="by_class" raises for a date column whose name is neither --DTC nor --STDTC.

docs.title: ADSL and OCCDS verbs follow the admiral rules they name
docs.text: The alpha audit of 2 November 2026 (package B) found that three verbs which cite admiral gave other answers than admiral. treatment_emergent flagged an AE with no start date as not emergent, read a start after TRTEDT as emergent with no window, and never looked at the end date. pick with order=["LSTALVDT"], mode="last" kept the first listed event, not the latest date, so LSTALVDT could be weeks early. recode always gave text, so recode_map={"MILD": 1, ...} made a text ASEVN. The recipes for SAFFL dropped placebo subjects (EXDOSE = 0) and left non-members blank. We decided that a verb which names an admiral function gives the admiral answer, and that the documented recipes state the SAP choice they make.

docs.title: The decision
docs.text:
• treatment_emergent follows derive_var_trtemfl. The first rule that applies decides: no TRTSDT gives null; an end date before TRTSDT gives null; no start date gives Y; a start on or after TRTSDT (plus offset_days) gives Y, and with end_window only up to TRTEDT plus the window, a null TRTEDT read as open; anything else gives null. end_date= is a required keyword (pass None to state that there is none), and trtedt= and end_window= come together, so the window is always written in the call.
  • pick decides across events as derive_vars_extreme_event. With a top-level order, every event's record competes on it and mode: order=["LSTALVDT"], mode="last" gives the latest date over all sources. A tie goes to the first listed event. With no top-level order, the first listed event with a record wins, as the admiral DTHCAUS template. Sorts keep the input order, so the result does not change between runs.
  • recode types the output from the map. Integer values give an integer column, floats (alone or with integers) a float column, other single kinds text. A map that mixes kinds raises DerivationError. A *N variable is Num in the ADaMIG, so a typing slip must stop the run, not give text.
  • SAFFL recipes state the exposure rule and give N. The recipes use the admiral template condition EXDOSE > 0 or (EXDOSE = 0 and EXTRT contains PLACEBO), case-insensitive, with a comment that the SAP decides. SAFFL and ITTFL use false_value="N", because ADaMIG 1.3 says a population flag cannot be blank. The flag default stays null.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep the old treatment_emergent signature and add the admiral rules behind a switch. Rejected: the old default gives a wrong TRTEMFL with no message, and a switch keeps it the default.
  • A default end_window of 30 days, as the admiral ADAE template. Rejected: the window is an SAP decision. The examples use 0, which keeps their results; the cheat sheet shows 30.
  • Keep the pick cascade and teach max_horizontal for LSTALVDT. Rejected: the call already reads as admiral's, and a programmer who ports admiral code gets the wrong date.
  • Change the flag default to N. Rejected: most flags (ABLFL, ANL01FL) are Y or null.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every treatment_emergent call must give end_date=; calls with trtedt= must give end_window=.
  • pick calls with a top-level order over several events can give another winner. Calls that need a cascade drop the top-level order and put it on each event.
  • recode with integer values now gives Int64, not text; code that compared the result with "1" must compare with 1.

docs.title: One flagged record per group, and units stated for QTc
docs.text: The alpha audit of 2 November 2026 (package C) found three verbs that gave a wrong flag or value with no message. baseline_flag chose by date only, so a NOT DONE record on the last date took the baseline flag and every record on that date got it. flag(criteria="last", where=) lost the flag when a record that failed where tied on order_by, so ABLFL, BASE and CHG were lost. qtc read RR in seconds while most studies hold it in ms, so QTcF was ten times too low. We decided that a baseline needs a result, that one record per group gets the flag, chosen as SAS LAST. chooses it, and that qtc reads RR in ms unless the call says otherwise.

docs.title: The decision
docs.text:
