If you are pulling in non-standard vendor files, rename and map columns directly inside the pipeline — no intermediate Polars .rename() call needed. .assign(target, source=...) is the canonical rename verb in both SDTM and ADaM; the ADaM .source(*cols) verb is the variadic pass-through for carrying already-named columns as-is:

import polars as pl

raw_labs = pl.read_csv("vendor_labs.csv")

# Rename non-standard columns inline, then continue the derivation
adlb = (
    raw_labs.adam.assign("USUBJID", source="Subject_ID")
    .assign("AVAL", source="Lab_Result")
    .baseline("BASE", aval="AVAL", baseline_flag="ABLFL")
    .to_frame()
)

Same verb, same spelling in SDTM:

dm = (
    raw_df.sdtm.assign("USUBJID", source="subject_id")
    .assign("SUBJID", source="subject_id")
    .to_frame()
)

Only fall back to raw Polars for pre-processing that genuinely cannot be expressed as a Fleet verb (e.g. pivoting wide vendor files, multi-file concatenation), and re-enter the Fleet pipeline immediately afterwards.

docs.title: Do not change a frame in place after a namespace call
docs.text: df.sdtm and df.adam keep the frame they saw at the first access. A Polars in-place method (insert_column, replace_column, df["X"] = ...) changes the frame, but not that copy. After a namespace call, add a column with with_columns (a new frame), not with an in-place method.

docs.title: Two races in DM: RACE = "MULTIPLE"
docs.text:
multiple_responses gives one row per response. Do not use it for DM RACE: DM has one record per subject. SDTMIG 3.4 section 4.2.8.3 puts MULTIPLE in RACE and each race in SUPPDM (RACE1, RACE2, ...):

races = pl.col("race").str.split("|")
ns = (
    raw_dm.with_columns(
        RACE1=races.list.get(0, null_on_oob=True),
        RACE2=races.list.get(1, null_on_oob=True),
    )
    .sdtm.assign("DOMAIN", value="DM")
    .assign("USUBJID", source="subject_id")
    .assign("RACE", source="RACE1")
    .condition_add("RACE", condition=pl.col("RACE2").is_not_null(), then_value="MULTIPLE")
    .nsv("RACE1", source="RACE1", label="Race 1", origin="Collected")
    .nsv("RACE2", source="RACE2", label="Race 2", origin="Collected")
)
suppdm = ns.export_supp()
dm = ns.to_frame().drop("RACE1", "RACE2")

docs.title: Cross-Domain Derivations with .pin()
docs.text: Many CDISC derivations require data from sibling domains — SDTM study day needs DM's RFSTDTC, ADaM datasets need ADSL columns like TRTSDT and population flags. Fleet's Pipeline Passport (.pin()) lets verbs see reference data without polluting the frame.

docs.title: Pinning a reference domain
docs.text:
# Build DM first
dm = dm_raw.sdtm.assign("DOMAIN", value="DM").to_frame()  # ...plus the rest of DM

# Pin DM to the VS pipeline — verbs can now resolve RFSTDTC
vs = (
    vs_raw.sdtm.assign("DOMAIN", value="VS")
    .assign("USUBJID", source="patient_number")
    .assign("VSTESTCD", source="vs_test_code")
    .assign("VSORRES", source="vs_result")
    .date("VSDTC", source="vs_date")
    .pin("DM", dm)  # ← attach reference (join_on="USUBJID" by default)
    .study_day("VSDY", date_col="VSDTC")  # ← consumes the pin
    .baseline_flag(
        "VSLOBXFL", date_col="VSDTC", testcd_col="VSTESTCD", ref_col="RFXSTDTC"
    )  # ← also consumes it
    .to_frame()
)

You don't see RFSTDTC in the call because .study_day() fills it in from its SDTM defaults: ref_pin="DM" and ref_col="RFSTDTC" — i.e. "look up RFSTDTC in the pinned DM, joined on the pin's key". Spelled out in full, the call above is:

vs_ns.study_day("VSDY", date_col="VSDTC", ref_pin="DM", ref_col="RFSTDTC")

On ADaM namespaces the same defaults become ref_pin="ADSL" / ref_col="TRTSDT". Resolution order: an explicit ref_df=/dm=/adsl= frame wins, then the pinned domain, then a ref_col already present in the frame — and a LookupError tells you what to pin when none of those hold.

The pinned DataFrame is not merged into the frame — it stays beside it. Verbs borrow what they need, compute, and drop temp columns. The output frame stays clean.

docs.title: Multiple pins
docs.text:
You can pin as many domains as you need:

ae = (
    ae_raw.sdtm.pin("DM", dm_df)  # join on USUBJID (default)
    .pin("TV", tv_df, join_on="VISITNUM")  # different join key
    .pin("EX", ex_df, join_on=["USUBJID", "EXTRT"])  # compound key
    .study_day("AESTDY", date_col="AESTDTC")  # ← reads DM.RFSTDTC via the DM pin
    .to_frame()
)

Datasets sharing a join key can be declared in one call — the keyword form mirrors the define.yaml inputs: block (kwarg name = dataset name):

adae = (
    ae_df.adam.occds("ADAE")
    .pin(ADSL=adsl_df, EX=ex_df)  # both join on USUBJID (default)
    .join_adsl("TRTSDT", "SAFFL")
    .to_frame()
)

Each verb names the pin it consumes (or falls back to its default ref_pin), and the join uses that pin's stored join_on — so the TV and EX pins above sit untouched until a visit- or exposure-consuming verb asks for them.

docs.title: ADaM: .join_adsl() and .study_day()
docs.text:
For ADaM datasets, pin ADSL and use .join_adsl() to carry forward columns, and .study_day() with the ADaM-standard default (TRTSDT):

adae = (
    ae_df.adam.occds("ADAE")
    .pin("ADSL", adsl)  # join_on="USUBJID" unless overridden
    .source("USUBJID")
    .join_adsl("TRTSDT", "TRTEDT", "SAFFL")  # left-join on the ADSL pin's key (USUBJID)
    .study_day("ASTDY", date_col="AESTDTC", ref_col="TRTSDT")
    .to_frame()
)

.join_adsl() has no by= parameter on purpose: the merge key is whatever the ADSL pin was registered with — USUBJID by default, or .pin("ADSL", adsl, join_on=["STUDYID", "USUBJID"]) for a compound key — so the join key is declared once, next to the data it belongs to. The pin-free alternative .merge_adsl(adsl, by=["USUBJID"], keep=[...]) takes an explicit frame and defaults by= to ["USUBJID"].

docs.title: FK validation
docs.text:
When a pin exists, Fleet checks foreign-key integrity at .to_frame(): every USUBJID of the final frame must be in the pinned DM (SDTM) or ADSL (ADaM). By default it emits a warning for orphan values; use .fk_policy() to make it strict or silent. The check runs once, on the final frame, with the last policy of the chain, so the order of pin, fk_policy and the verbs does not matter. With trial-design pins, SDTM also checks the keys below.

ae = (
    ae_raw.sdtm.pin("DM", dm)
    .assign("USUBJID", source="patient_number")
    .fk_policy("error")  # raise on FK violations, checked against DM at to_frame()
    .to_frame()
)

Three SDTM rules follow the IG. ETCD UNPLAN is legal in SE, so it is not an orphan of TE. VISITNUM and VISIT orphans stay warnings under "error", because TV holds planned visits only and an unscheduled visit is legal. EPOCH is checked against a pinned TA, which holds EPOCH (TE has none).

docs.title: Lineage tracing
docs.text:
Every derivation — including cross-domain pin access — is recorded automatically. Print the origin of every derived variable with the .trail() verb (detailed in the Observability section below), without breaking the chain:

ae = (
    ae_raw.sdtm.assign("USUBJID", source="patient_number")
    .assign("AESTDTC", source="ae_start_date")
    .pin("DM", dm)
    .study_day("AESTDY", date_col="AESTDTC")
    .trail()  # prints the origin table; pipeline continues
    .to_frame()
)

The cross-domain pin is attributed in the Origin column as DM.RFSTDTC.

docs.title: Pipeline Debugging & Observability
docs.text: Fleet pipelines are lazy — all derivations accumulate until .to_frame() collects the result. This can make it hard to pinpoint which step introduced bad data or types — or to see where each variable came from. Three chainable verbs help:

docs.title: .inspect() — Hard Checkpoint
docs.text:
Materialises the pipeline at that point, prints schema, shape, and first rows, then returns a fresh namespace wrapping the collected frame. The pipeline resumes from this checkpoint.

adsl = (
    dm.adam.adsl.source("USUBJID")
    .first_date("TRTSDT", from_dataset=ex, date_col="EXSTDTC")
    .inspect(prefix="After TRTSDT")  # prints and checkpoints
    .last_date("TRTEDT", from_dataset=ex, date_col="EXENDTC")
    .duration("TRTDURD", start="TRTSDT", end="TRTEDT")
    .to_frame()
)

docs.title: .explain() — Query Plan
docs.text:
Prints the Polars logical plan without materialising. Useful for understanding how Polars optimises the accumulated derivation pipeline.

advs = (
    vs_raw.adam.source("USUBJID")
    .derivation("AVAL", expression="VSSTRESN")
    .explain()  # shows optimised plan
    .to_frame()
)

docs.title: .trail() — Variable Origin
docs.text:
Prints a table of every derived variable: the verb that produced it and the source columns it consumed, including cross-domain pin sources shown as DOMAIN.COLUMN. Nothing is materialised — the trail is metadata captured automatically on every verb — so it can sit anywhere in the chain, though it is most complete just before .to_frame().

ae = (
    ae_raw.sdtm.assign("DOMAIN", value="AE")
    .assign("USUBJID", source="patient_number")
    .assign("AESTDTC", source="ae_start_date")
    .pin("DM", dm)
    .study_day("AESTDY", date_col="AESTDTC")
    .trail()  # prints the table below, pipeline continues
    .to_frame()
)

Variable trail (4 derivation(s)):
┌───┬──────────┬────────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────┐
│ # ┆ Variable ┆ Verb           ┆ Origin              ┆ Domain │
╞═══╪══════════╪════════════════╪═════════════════════╪════════╡
│ 1 ┆ DOMAIN   ┆ assign         ┆ (literal)           ┆ —      │
│ 2 ┆ USUBJID  ┆ assign         ┆ patient_number      ┆ AE     │
│ 3 ┆ AESTDTC  ┆ assign         ┆ ae_start_date       ┆ AE     │
│ 4 ┆ AESTDY   ┆ study_day      ┆ AESTDTC, DM.RFSTDTC ┆ AE     │
└───┴──────────┴────────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────┘

Variables with no source column (e.g. hardcoded constants) are marked (literal); a variable derived more than once appears once per derivation, in pipeline order. Passthrough columns that no verb touched are not listed.

All three verbs are available on df.sdtm, df.adam, and all ADaM sub-namespaces.

docs.title: Coming from SAS
docs.text:
This page lists the places where Fleet and SAS can give different results on the same data. For each one it gives the SAS rule, the Fleet rule and a sample that runs. The decision records (ADRs) give the reasons.

The samples share this setup:

import polars as pl

import fleet

docs.title: Missing values in a condition
docs.text:
SAS: a missing numeric value is lower than every number. IF AVAL < 5 is true for a missing AVAL, so an IF/ELSE gives the record the "true" branch.

Fleet: a condition on a missing value is missing (ADR-0033, as admiral). criterion() gives a null CRITyFL and CRITyFN on that record. When the SAP says "missing is not met", write it in the condition with .fill_null(False).

adlb = pl.from_repr("""
┌─────────┬──────┐
│ USUBJID ┆ AVAL │
│ ---     ┆ ---  │
│ str     ┆ f64  │
╞═════════╪══════╡
│ S1      ┆ 3.0  │
│ S2      ┆ null │
└─────────┴──────┘
""")

crit = adlb.adam.criterion(1, condition=pl.col("AVAL") < 5, description="AVAL < 5").to_frame()
crit["CRIT1FL"].to_list()  # ['Y', None]; SAS IF/ELSE gives 'Y' for S2 too

docs.title: Sort order of a missing key
docs.text:
SAS: PROC SORT puts a missing value first (it is the lowest value), and last with DESCENDING.

Fleet: two rules, each stated in its docstring.

  • The flag verbs (flag(criteria="first"/"last"), flag_first) follow admiral: a missing value sorts last in each key (ADR-0020). A QC program with PROC SORT and LAST. can pick another record when a key is missing.
  • nodup() translates PROC SORT NODUPKEY, so it follows SAS: a missing value is the lowest value (ADR-0023). Ties keep their input order, as EQUALS.
adae = pl.from_repr("""
┌─────────┬────────┬────────┐
│ USUBJID ┆ AETERM ┆ AESEVN │
│ ---     ┆ ---    ┆ ---    │
│ str     ┆ str    ┆ i64    │
╞═════════╪════════╪════════╡
│ S1      ┆ RASH   ┆ null   │
│ S1      ┆ RASH   ┆ 2      │
└─────────┴────────┴────────┘
""")

worst = adae.adam.nodup(
    subset=["USUBJID", "AETERM"], order_by=["AESEVN"], keep="first", descending=True
).to_frame()
worst["AESEVN"].to_list()  # [2]: as PROC SORT BY DESCENDING AESEVN NODUPKEY

docs.title: Rounding of a printed value
docs.text:
SAS: ROUND(31.25, 0.1) gives 31.3: a tie rounds half away from zero.

Fleet: the same rule for every printed cell (ADR-0037). The ARD keeps the unrounded value; only the printed text is rounded. A Python f-string rounds the binary value and can print 31.2: do not use one for a table cell.

from fleet.tlg import apply_fmt_fn

apply_fmt_fn(5 / 16 * 100, "xx.x")  # '31.3', as SAS ROUND

docs.title: Merge
docs.text:
SAS: MERGE a b(KEEP=USUBJID AGE); BY USUBJID; keeps every column of a. A column on both sides takes the value of b with no message.

Fleet: merge(keep=) limits the right dataset in the same way, and every column of the chain stays. A non-key column on both sides raises and names the column: drop or rename it first (ADR-0032, as admiral). merge_adsl and join_adsl also raise when ADSL has more than one record for a subject.

ae = pl.from_repr("""
┌─────────┬──────────┐
│ USUBJID ┆ AETERM   │
│ ---     ┆ ---      │
│ str     ┆ str      │
╞═════════╪══════════╡
│ S1      ┆ HEADACHE │
└─────────┴──────────┘
""")
dm = pl.from_repr("""
┌─────────┬─────┬─────┐
│ USUBJID ┆ AGE ┆ SEX │
│ ---     ┆ --- ┆ --- │
│ str     ┆ i64 ┆ str │
╞═════════╪═════╪═════╡
│ S1      ┆ 63  ┆ F   │
└─────────┴─────┴─────┘
""")

ae_dm = ae.sdtm.merge(dm, on="USUBJID", keep=["AGE"]).to_frame()
ae_dm.columns  # ['USUBJID', 'AETERM', 'AGE']

docs.title: Dates
docs.text:
SAS: an informat reads the text you name (yymmdd10., date9.). A partial date has no SAS date value.

Fleet: a --DTC column is ISO 8601 text (pl.String). .sdtm.date() never guesses: a slash date or a two-digit year raises until format= names the layout, as an explicit SAS informat does. A partial date stays partial in --DTC, and a day count on it is missing (ADR-0011). Imputation happens only when you ask for it, on a *DT target (impute=, highest=).

raw = pl.from_repr("""
┌────────────┐
│ start      │
│ ---        │
│ str        │
╞════════════╡
│ 2024-03-15 │
│ 2024-03    │
└────────────┘
""")

ex = raw.sdtm.date("EXSTDTC", source="start").to_frame()
ex["EXSTDTC"].to_list()  # ['2024-03-15', '2024-03']: the partial date stays partial

docs.title: Comparing Datasets
docs.text:
Every QC step ends with the same question: is this dataset the same as that one, and if not, where exactly does it differ? SAS answers it with PROC COMPARE. Fleet answers it with compare — one engine in pure Polars, reachable as a Python function, as a pipeline verb, and as a CLI command.

A compare pairs two datasets observation by observation on their keys and variable by variable on their names, then reports where they differ. It is distinct from validation, which checks one dataset against CDISC conformance rules.

Term Meaning Base The reference dataset the comparison is measured against (production, legacy SAS, last release). Candidate The dataset being measured against the base (the independent QC programming, the migrated output). Keys The variables that together identify one observation on each side. Mandatory; never looked up. Comparison report The outcome: which variables and observations were common or one-sided, and every value that differed.

docs.title: Three surfaces, one engine
docs.text:
From Python, fleet.compare takes DataFrames or LazyFrames on either side and returns a ComparisonReport. Differences never raise — the report says what was found:

import fleet

report = fleet.compare(adae_prod, adae_qc, keys=["USUBJID", "AESEQ"])
report.print_report()
assert report.is_equal, report.raised_flags

At the end of a pipeline, the .compare() verb is available on df.sdtm, df.adam, df.adam.adsl and df.adam.occds. The chain is the candidate and the argument is the base; the verb prints the report, keeps it on the namespace as last_comparison, and returns a namespace copy so the chain continues:

adae_qc = (
    ae_df.adam.occds.source("USUBJID")
    .source("AESEQ")
    .compare(adae_prod, keys=["USUBJID", "AESEQ"])
    .to_frame()
)

From a shell, fleet compare loads both files through the raw-data loader (parquet, CSV, and XPT or sas7bdat with the io extra), prints the report, and turns the verdict into the exit code:

uv run fleet compare adae_prod.parquet adae_qc.parquet --keys USUBJID,AESEQ
uv run fleet compare legacy/adae.xpt outputs/adam/adae.parquet --keys USUBJID,AESEQ --all
Exit code Meaning 0 The datasets are equal. 1 The datasets differ; the report on stdout says where. 2 The comparison could not run: unreadable file, missing or duplicate keys, a negative tolerance, a --variables list that names only keys, or an --out or --report path that cannot be written. The reason is on stderr.

A compare that checks no values still gives a verdict. When the two sides share only their keys, the verdict follows the observations: the same key values on both sides are EQUAL, a one-sided key or variable is NOT EQUAL. When both sides have no observations, the verdict is EQUAL. In both cases the report warns above the first number, so an EQUAL that checked no values never reads as a full pass (ADR-0004).

--keys is required. --by TRT01P sections the report per BY group and --allow-duplicates pairs duplicate keys by position. --pairs and --variables rename and restrict what is compared. --abs-tol, --rel-tol and --ignore-trailing-whitespace widen equality (see tolerances and whitespace). --all lifts the print limits so every unequal value is listed. --report adae_compare.html writes the HTML report for a reviewer. --format json prints one JSON document and nothing else on stdout, and --out differences.parquet writes the complete value listing; both are described under machine-readable outputs. See the CLI reference for the full usage.

docs.title: What the report contains
docs.text:
The text report follows the PROC COMPARE section order, so a SAS programmer reads it without a legend:

  1. Data set summary — name, observations and variables per side, the keys, and the settings line naming the equality rule in effect (exact, or the tolerances and the whitespace rule).
  2. Variables summary — variables in common, in the base only, in the candidate only, type conflicts, dtype differences.
  3. Observation summary — matched observations and the key values of the ones found on one side only.
  4. Values summary — how many values differ, per variable.
  5. Summary statistics — for each differing numeric variable, how far apart the two sides are (see summary statistics).
  6. Value listing — every unequal value, grouped per observation so one subject's differences read together, with the base value, the candidate value, and the difference and percent difference for numeric variables.
  7. Verdict — EQUAL, or NOT EQUAL followed by the raised flags.

The report object carries the same content as data: report.listing is a long Polars frame (keys, group, variable, base, candidate, difference, percent_difference) that is never truncated, report.statistics is the summary statistics frame, and report.flags replaces SAS's SYSINFO integer with names — base_only_variables, candidate_only_variables, type_conflicts, base_only_observations, candidate_only_observations, values_differ, duplicate_keys, base_only_groups, candidate_only_groups. report.is_equal is true only when no flag is raised. report.warnings holds the lines every renderer prints above the report — today only the duplicate-key one.

docs.title: Summary statistics
docs.text:
Counting differences says how many, not whether the candidate runs systematically a little high or scatters at random. report.statistics says which: one row per differing variable and, for a numeric one, the shape of both sides, of their difference, and of that difference as a percentage of the base.

report = fleet.compare(advs_prod, advs_qc, keys=["USUBJID", "PARAMCD", "AVISITN"])
offset = report.statistics.filter(pl.col("difference_mean").abs() > 0.5)
Column Content variable The differing variable, by its base name, in compared order. differences How many matched observations differ on it. base_n, base_mean, base_std, base_min, base_max The base values. candidate_n … candidate_max The same five, of the candidate values. difference_n … difference_max The same five, of candidate − base. percent_difference_n … percent_difference_max The same five, of (candidate − base) ÷ base × 100.

Two things decide what the numbers mean:

  • The measures span every matched observation, not only the unequal ones. A mean difference near zero over a thousand observations with three differences reads as noise; a mean difference of exactly 0.5 across all of them reads as an offset. Only observations null, NaN or infinite on either side are dropped, because a difference needs two finite values — which is why n can be smaller than the matched count, and smaller again for the percent, which drops a zero base as the listing does. No measure is ever NaN or infinite, so the text report, the HTML page and the JSON document show the same numbers.
  • Only numeric variables carry them. A string, a date or a boolean contributes its differences count and nulls for the rest; there is no mean of "F" against "M".

The statistics are on every surface: their own section in the text report after the values summary, the statistics key of the JSON document, and a table at the top of each variable's block in the HTML page. An equal comparison has an empty frame and an empty section.

Deliberately absent are PROC COMPARE's correlation, R² and t statistic: they answer a modelling question rather than a QC one, and the value listing answers the QC one exactly.

docs.title: The HTML report
docs.text:
A study lead reviews without a Python environment. report.to_html() renders one self-contained page and report.save_html_report(path) writes it; from the shell, fleet compare --report adae_compare.html does the same next to the text report:

uv run fleet compare adae_prod.parquet adae_qc.parquet --keys USUBJID,AESEQ --report build/adae_compare.html

The page opens offline: its style is embedded and it fetches no script, font or image. It reads top-down the way a review goes:

  1. Verdict — EQUAL or NOT EQUAL, with the one-line summary and the raised flags.
  2. Chips — one per raised flag, so structural problems are visible before value details: the variables found on one side only, the type conflicts with their dtypes, the observations on one side only (the first few named by their key values), how many values differ. Dtype differences appear as an information chip, never as a finding.
  3. Summary — name, observations and variables per side, the keys, the equality rule in effect, and how many observations matched.
  4. Observations on one side only — the key values of every observation found only in the base or only in the candidate.
  5. Unequal values — only the mismatched observations, one collapsible block per differing variable. Each block opens on the variable's summary statistics, then lists every unequal row: the key values, the base value and the candidate value side by side with both cells highlighted, and the difference and percent difference for numeric variables. Blocks start open when there are five or fewer, closed beyond that, so a report over fifty variables stays navigable.

The page is never truncated: every unequal value is on it, whatever max_print the comparison ran with. With BY groups it gains a Groups section with the per-group counts and sections the unequal values per group. The summary statistics span all groups, so the page then draws them once per variable, above the group sections, with the caption "over all groups". A listed value that would read the same as another one is quoted: "M " against M, "null" against a missing null, "" against null. The text report quotes the same way; the JSON document and the parquet keep the raw values. For listings beyond a few thousand rows, the parquet listing is the better archive.

docs.title: Machine-readable outputs
docs.text:
An agent or a CI job consumes the comparison without parsing prose. report.to_json() renders one JSON document, report.save_json(path) writes it, and report.save_listing(path) writes the complete value listing as parquet. From the shell, fleet compare --format json prints the document and nothing else on stdout (the exit code is still the verdict, and a comparison that could not run still leaves stdout empty with the reason on stderr), and --out writes the listing:

uv run fleet compare adae_prod.parquet adae_qc.parquet --keys USUBJID,AESEQ --format json > adae_compare.json
uv run fleet compare adae_prod.parquet adae_qc.parquet --keys USUBJID,AESEQ --out build/adae_differences.parquet

docs.title: The JSON contract
docs.text:
Field names mirror the report attributes. The document is additive-only within a major version, in the spirit of ADR 0001: keys may be added, never removed or renamed, so a comparison view built on them (the editor extension is the intended consumer) declares a minimum Fleet version and no ceiling. The top-level keys, in order (fleet.comparison.JSON_KEYS):

Key Content is_equal The verdict: true only when no flag is raised. summary The one-line summary, as report.summary. flags The raised flags, in their documented order. warnings The lines every renderer prints above the report; empty on an ordinary comparison. datasets base and candidate, each with name, rows and variables. variables common, compared, base_only, candidate_only, then type_conflicts and dtype_differences as {variable, base_dtype, candidate_dtype} with the dtypes as text. observations matched, base_only, candidate_only, the one-sided key values as base_only_keys and candidate_only_keys (capped at the per-variable print limit; truncated says whether a cap applied), base_duplicates and candidate_duplicates, the per-group counts as per_group, and the one-sided group labels as base_only_groups and candidate_only_groups. values per_variable as {variable, differences}, variables_with_differences, observations_with_differences, total_differences, per_group, and within_tolerance (values equal under a tolerance or ignore_trailing_whitespace but not exactly equal). statistics One object per differing variable, with the columns of fleet.comparison.STATISTICS_COLUMNS; the measures are null for a variable that is not numeric. See summary statistics. listing columns, rows (one object per differing value, within the print limits), shown, total and truncated. settings Every option the comparison ran with: keys, by, pairs, variables, abs_tol, rel_tol, ignore_trailing_whitespace, allow_duplicates, max_print, base_name, candidate_name. version The Fleet version that produced the report.

The document is strict JSON: non-finite numbers are null and temporal key values are ISO 8601 strings. max_print governs the listing inside the document exactly as it governs the text (--all or max_print=None lifts it); the parquet listing is never truncated.

import json

document = json.loads(report.to_json())
if not document["is_equal"]:
    for row in document["listing"]["rows"]:
        print(row["USUBJID"], row["variable"], row["base"], "->", row["candidate"])

docs.title: The parquet listing
docs.text: save_listing writes report.listing as is: the key columns in their own dtypes, then group (String, the BY group label or null), variable, base and candidate (String), difference and percent_difference (Float64). An equal comparison writes an empty frame with the same schema, so a downstream scan_parquet always finds the documented columns.

docs.title: Rules of equality
docs.text:
• Keys are mandatory and must be unique on each side. A missing or duplicated key stops the compare with a ComparisonError that names the side and the offending key values, because a broken key is the first thing to fix. allow_duplicates is the deliberate way past it.
  • Equality is exact by default. Null equals null, NaN equals NaN, and null against NaN differs, so a missing value that became a NaN is surfaced. Tolerances widen it on the numeric variables and trailing-whitespace stripping on the strings; the null and NaN rule holds under both.
  • Same kind, different dtype is information, not a failure. An Int64 next to a Float64, a String next to a Categorical, or a Date next to a Datetime is compared by value after casting to a common type and listed as a dtype difference. A numeric next to a string is a type conflict: listed, not compared.
  • A blank is not a missing value unless you say so. A SAS file reads a blank as null, so XPT against Parquet needs nothing. A file from another tool can keep "" (an R data frame without convert_blanks_to_na), and "" against null differs by default. blank_is_missing=True (or --blank-is-missing) reads "" as null on both sides, keys included, and the settings line says blank equals missing.
  • A CSV file holds no types. fleet compare reads a CSV side as text and types each column across both sides: the other side's type when that side is not a CSV file; otherwise text when a value on either side has a leading zero or is not a number, and a number in every other case. So SITEID 001 against 1 differs, and AVAL 1.10 against 1.1 is equal, as in PROC COMPARE. --text LBORRES keeps a column text, the $ informat. The text report starts with the type each CSV column was read as.
  • Row order and column order are ignored. A re-sorted or re-ordered dataset is not a different dataset.
  • Print limits only affect what is rendered. By default the text report and the JSON document show 50 differences per variable and 500 overall; max_print=None (or --all) shows everything. The listing frame and the parquet always hold every difference.

docs.title: Tolerances and trailing whitespace
docs.text:
A migration programmer comparing Fleet output against a legacy SAS dataset has to absorb engine noise without hiding a real difference. Three options do that, and they are the same three on every surface:

Option Applies to Effect abs_tol / --abs-tol Numeric variables Absolute tolerance. Default 0.0 — exact. rel_tol / --rel-tol Numeric variables Relative tolerance, as a fraction of the base value. Default 0.0 — exact. ignore_trailing_whitespace / --ignore-trailing-whitespace String variables and string keys Strip trailing whitespace from both sides before comparing. Default False.

A numeric pair differs when the absolute difference exceeds max(abs_tol, rel_tol × |base|), so the wider of the two tolerances is the one that decides. The relative tolerance anchors on the base, because the base is the reference the candidate is measured against — this follows PROC COMPARE and deliberately not Polars' testing helper, which anchors on its right-hand frame. The choice is visible: at rel_tol=0.095 a base of 100 against a candidate of 110 differs (10 > 9.5), while the same pair with the sides swapped is equal (10 ≤ 10.45).

report = fleet.compare(
    advs_legacy,
    advs_fleet,
    keys=["USUBJID", "PARAMCD", "AVISITN"],
    rel_tol=1e-9,
    ignore_trailing_whitespace=True,
)

uv run fleet compare legacy/advs.xpt outputs/adam/advs.parquet \
  --keys USUBJID,PARAMCD,AVISITN --rel-tol 1e-9 --ignore-trailing-whitespace

What the options do not change:

  • Exact stays the default. Both tolerances are 0.0 and whitespace counts until you say otherwise.
  • Tolerances only reach the numeric variables. A string, a date or a boolean is compared exactly however wide abs_tol is, and stripping only reaches the string ones.
  • Nulls and NaN keep their rule. Null still equals null, NaN still equals NaN, and null against NaN — or NaN against a number — still differs, however wide the tolerance. A NaN is never within a tolerance of a number. Infinity follows R all.equal: inf equals inf, and inf against a number or against -inf differs in every mode.
  • Only trailing whitespace is ignored. "M " equals "M" when asked; " M" never does.
  • The listing shows the values as they are. A difference that survives the tolerance is reported with the original base and candidate values, unstripped.
  • What the rule absorbed is counted. report.values.within_tolerance (and within_tolerance in the JSON values block) counts the values equal under the rule but not exactly equal, as the PROC COMPARE note does. The text report then says All compared values are within the rule in effect; 3 of them are not exactly equal.
  • A tolerant comparison is arithmetic in Float64. Integers and decimals beyond 2**53 are therefore compared at that precision; the exact default compares them in their own dtype.

The rule in effect is on every surface: the settings line of the text report (Settings: abs_tol=1e-09, rel_tol=0, ignoring trailing whitespace, or Settings: exact), the header of the HTML report, and the settings block of the JSON document as the three raw fields.

The option also strips the string keys, before the duplicate-key check. A SAS-padded USUBJID "01-701-1015 " then pairs with "01-701-1015" from Fleet. Two keys that differ only in trailing blanks are duplicates. The listing shows the keys stripped.

docs.title: Duplicate keys
docs.text:
Keys that do not identify one observation per side stop the compare, because a broken key is usually the bug. When the duplication is expected — a dataset with no sequence variable, a legacy extract — allow_duplicates forces the comparison through:

report = fleet.compare(adae_prod, adae_qc, keys=["USUBJID"], allow_duplicates=True)

uv run fleet compare adae_prod.parquet adae_qc.parquet --keys USUBJID --allow-duplicates

Duplicates then pair by their position within each key group: the first base observation for USUBJID=01 against the first candidate one, the second against the second, and so on. An unpaired one — three on the base, two on the candidate — is reported as an observation found on one side only.

That is a weaker guarantee than pairing on keys, so it is never silent:

  • the observation summary counts the duplicates per side;
  • the duplicate_keys flag is raised, so the comparison is never is_equal;
  • report.warnings carries a line every renderer prints above the report, and the JSON document repeats it under warnings.

Row order stops being irrelevant under the override, and only within a duplicated key group: which base observation meets which candidate one is decided by the order the two datasets arrive in.

docs.title: BY groups
docs.text:
A reviewer looking at a study with several treatment arms wants to know where the differences are, not just how many. by sections the report:

report = fleet.compare(adsl_prod, adsl_qc, keys="USUBJID", by="TRT01P")
report.observations.per_group  # group, matched, base_only, candidate_only
report.values.per_group  # group, variables_with_differences, observations_with_differences, differences

uv run fleet compare adsl_prod.parquet adsl_qc.parquet --keys USUBJID --by TRT01P

The BY variables are prepended to the keys automatically, so they need not be repeated in keys (repeating them is harmless). Everything else follows from that:

  • Every difference carries its group in the listing's group column, labelled TRT01P=A (and TRT01P=A, AVISIT=2 with several BY variables), and the listing is sorted by group first.
  • The observation summary and the values summary are reported per group as well as in total, in the text report, the JSON document and the HTML page.
  • A group present on one side only raises base_only_groups or candidate_only_groups and is listed by name, so a missing arm reads as a missing arm rather than as a thousand missing observations.
  • The verdict stays global. is_equal is still true only when no flag is raised anywhere.

docs.title: Variable pairs and restriction
docs.text:
Two datasets rarely line up by name alone. A legacy extract calls a variable WEIGHT where the candidate calls it WT, and a candidate that is still being written has columns nobody wants compared yet. pairs and variables say so:

report = fleet.compare(
    advs_legacy,
    advs_wip,
    keys=["USUBJID", "PARAMCD"],
    pairs={"WEIGHT": "WT"},  # base name: candidate name
    variables=["WEIGHT", "AVISIT"],  # base names
)

uv run fleet compare legacy/advs.xpt outputs/adam/advs.parquet \
  --keys USUBJID,PARAMCD --pairs WEIGHT=WT --variables WEIGHT,AVISIT

pairs maps base names to candidate names, on top of the automatic name matching rather than instead of it: everything not named in pairs still matches by name. A paired variable is compared by value and no longer reported missing on either side, and the report — the values summary, the listing, the HTML blocks — names it by its base name throughout. A pair is otherwise an ordinary common variable: same kind but a different dtype is a dtype difference, a different kind is a type conflict.

A pair whose candidate variable is absent reports the base one as missing from the candidate, exactly as an unpaired variable would. A pair whose base variable the base does not carry, one that renames a key, and two pairs pointing at the same candidate variable are refused with a ComparisonError: the pairing could not be honoured as written. So is a pair whose candidate variable a base variable of the same name also matches by name: with base A and B, pairs={"A": "B"} is refused, and the swap pairs={"A": "B", "B": "A"} is legal. A candidate variable that no pair uses and that no base variable matches by name is reported as extra: with pairs={"AVAL": "RESULT"}, a candidate AVAL is a candidate-only variable.

variables restricts the universe, in base names. What is outside the list is ignored entirely, on both sides: not compared, and not reported as missing or extra either — a work-in-progress candidate is checked on the columns that are finished without its unfinished ones raising a flag. What is on the list still is: a restricted variable the candidate does not carry is still reported as missing from it. Keys are never restricted; they pair observations whatever the list says. A restriction naming a variable neither side carries is refused, because a comparison that silently compares nothing would report two datasets as equal.

Both options are recorded in report.settings (pairs and variables) and shown wherever a run is described: the data set summary of the text report, the header of the HTML page, and the settings block of the JSON document.

docs.title: Gating a pipeline on the outcome
docs.text:
The verb speaks the same failure vocabulary as .validate():

on_fail Behaviour when the datasets differ "warn" (default) Emit a UserWarning and continue the chain. "raise" Raise ComparisonFailed, a subclass of ComparisonError (a FleetError). "ignore" No warning and no error. The report is still printed and stays on last_comparison. 
adsl = (
    dm_df.adam.adsl.source("USUBJID")
    .assign("STUDYID", value="MYSTUDY01")
    .compare(adsl_prod, keys="USUBJID", on_fail="raise")
    .to_frame()
)

Any other value fails fast with a DerivationError, exactly as .validate() does.

docs.title: Where it stops today
docs.text: The engine compares values, not metadata: a Polars frame carries no labels, formats or lengths, so comparing those would need a define.yaml-aware mode. Keys are mandatory on all three surfaces — there is no positional matching, and no lookup of keys from define.yaml or the study configuration. A comparison takes exactly two datasets, never a batch of directories. A SAS special missing value (.A to .Z and ._) in an XPT or SAS7BDAT file reads as null and its letter is lost, so .A against .R compares equal, which SAS PROC COMPARE reports as unequal. The compare spec tracks what is deliberately left out and what may follow it, including an MCP tool and a diff view in the editor extension built on the JSON contract above.

docs.title: Custom Validation Rules
docs.text: Custom rules are Fleet's extension mechanism for CORE — start with Validation with CORE for the base engine setup and the official rule sets. When the standard CDISC CORE conformance rules do not cover a study-specific requirement — a sponsor SOP constraint, an FDA Technical Conformance Guide (TCG) gap, a protocol-specific range check, or ADaM checks while the official ADaMIG rule set remains unpublished — you author custom rules and run them next to the official rules.

docs.title: Official and custom rules both run
docs.text:
CORE runs only the -lr rules when it gets a rules directory: one AE file ran 430 official rules without -lr and only the 2 custom rules with it. So Fleet runs the engine twice per standard when custom rules are set:

  1. one run without -lr: the official CDISC rules,
  2. one run with -lr: the custom rules only.

The findings of both runs join into one report per dataset. Each finding names its source, official or custom:

1. [CORE-000718] (official) AESTDTC falls after  AEENDTC.
2. [FLEET-AE-001] (custom) AESEV is missing for a serious AE

The source is also on ValidationIssue.source, in the HTML reports, and in the MCP fleet_validate output. Without custom rules, the engine runs once per standard.

docs.title: When to write custom rules
docs.text:
• Sponsor SOPs require checks not covered by CDISC CORE (e.g. mandatory SUPPQUAL variables).
  • FDA TCG requirements that have not yet been formalised as CORE rules.
  • Protocol-specific constraints such as custom reference ranges, visit windows, or dose limits.
  • Interim quality gates during study setup before official validation.

docs.title: 1. Configure the custom rules directory
docs.text:
In your study_config.yaml, set the custom_rules path:

validation:
  custom_rules: metadata/custom_rules  # directory for your .yaml rule files

fleet init cfg sets this up by default. The engine loads all .yaml files in this directory.

docs.title: 2. Scaffold a new rule
docs.text:
# Auto-increments ID: FLEET-AE-001, FLEET-AE-002, …
uv run fleet add-rule --domain AE --description "AESEV must be populated when AESER = Y"

# Custom prefix
uv run fleet add-rule --domain AE --prefix ACME --description "Severity required for serious AEs"

# Explicit ID (skips auto-increment)
uv run fleet add-rule --domain VS --id ACME-VS-010 --description "VSORRES range check"

# Output to a specific directory (overrides study_config)
uv run fleet add-rule --domain AE --description "Custom check" --output ./my_rules/

docs.title: 3. Edit the Check block
docs.text:
Open the generated YAML and fill in your validation logic in the Check: section:

Check:
  all:
    - name: AESER
      operator: equal_to
      value: "Y"
      value_is_literal: true
    - name: AESEV
      operator: empty

docs.title: 4. Run validation
docs.text:
# Inline in a pipeline: inside the study, validation.custom_rules applies
ae = raw_df.sdtm.assign("DOMAIN", value="AE").validate("AE").to_frame()

# Or name the directory explicitly
ae = (
    raw_df.sdtm.assign("DOMAIN", value="AE")
    .validate("AE", custom_rules="metadata/custom_rules")
    .to_frame()
)

# Or via the ValidationService
from fleet.validation.service import ValidationService

svc = ValidationService()
result = svc.validate_sdtm(ae, domain="AE", version="3.4", custom_rules="metadata/custom_rules")
result.print_report()

A relative rules path is relative to the working directory, as the dataset path is. Fleet resolves it before the engine starts in its own folder.

docs.title: 5. Read the rule counts
docs.text:
The custom rules run in their own engine run. The report counts what that run did with the rules, apart from the data findings:

Rules (engine run, custom): 1 executed, 1 skipped, 1 could not run, 1 not loaded

fleet validate and the HTML report also name the rules:

Rule problems in the sdtmig engine run (not data findings; exit code kept):
  Could not run (custom): FLEET-AE-002 (Rule contains invalid operator)
  Not loaded (custom): broken.yaml
  • Could not run: the engine reports EXECUTION_ERROR for the rule, for example an unknown operator. The reason comes from the engine.
  • Not loaded: a YAML file that does not parse, or a rule ID that is absent from the engine report.
  • Skipped: the engine skips a rule when no dataset is in its scope, or when a variable the rule names is absent from the dataset. This is correct for a permissive variable that was not collected, so a skip is counted, never listed. Check the variable names of a rule that you expect to run.

Rule problems do not change the status or the exit code. A true finding is always kept, whatever its message says.

docs.title: Rule anatomy
docs.text:
A custom rule follows the same YAML schema as CDISC CORE rules. Here is an annotated example:

Core:
  Id: FLEET-AE-001          # Unique ID (auto-generated by fleet add-rule)
  Status: Draft
  Version: "1"

Rule Type: Record Data       # Record-level check

Scope:
  Classes:
    Include: [ALL]           # Every class; Domains below sets the scope
  Domains:
    Include: [AE]            # Restrict to the AE domain

Check:                       # The validation logic (what you write)
  all:
    - name: AESER
      operator: equal_to
      value: "Y"
      value_is_literal: true
    - name: AESEV
      operator: empty

Outcome:
  Message: >-
    AESEV is empty for a record where AESER = 'Y'. Serious adverse events
    must have severity documented.
  Output Variables: [USUBJID, AETERM, AESER, AESEV]

Description: >-
  AESEV must be populated when AESER = 'Y'.

Authorities:
  - Organization: Fleet
    Standards:
      - Name: SDTMIG
        Version: "3.4"
        References:
          - Origin: Sponsor SOP
            Rule Identifier:
              Id: FLEET-AE-001
              Version: "1"
            Version: "1"
    Category:                # Required for a sponsor (custom) organization
      Purpose: Sponsor SOP compliance
      Keywords: [AE]

Sensitivity: Record
Executability: Fully Executable

docs.title: The check DSL
docs.text:
CDISC CORE rules use a JSON/YAML check DSL built from composable operators:

Combinator Meaning all All conditions must be true (AND) any At least one condition is true (OR) not Negates the enclosed condition

Each leaf condition specifies a variable name, an operator, and optionally a value:

Check:
  all:
    - name: AESEV
      operator: is_contained_by
      value: ["MILD", "MODERATE", "SEVERE"]
    - name: AESER
      operator: equal_to
      value: "Y"
      value_is_literal: true

docs.title: Available operators
docs.text:
Operator Description equal_to Exact match not_equal_to Not equal empty Variable is null/blank non_empty Variable has a value less_than / greater_than Numeric/date comparison less_than_or_equal_to / greater_than_or_equal_to Inclusive comparison contains / does_not_contain Substring check is_contained_by Value is in a list starts_with / ends_with Prefix/suffix check matches_regex Regex pattern match date_less_than / date_greater_than Date comparison

For the full operator reference, see the CDISC CORE Rule Editor.

docs.title: Configuration and resolution order
docs.text:
Fleet resolves custom rules from multiple sources. The first match wins:

  1. Explicit custom_rules= parameter on .validate() or ValidationService methods.
  2. validation.custom_rules in study_config.yaml (team-wide default). The .validate() verb finds the study config from the working directory.
  3. None — no custom rules are loaded.

A directory that does not exist is refused before the engine starts: the verb raises ValidationSetupError. The report header shows the directory used and its source.

docs.title: Storing custom rules
docs.text:
Place custom rule files in the configured directory (default: metadata/custom_rules/):

my_study/
  study_config.yaml
  metadata/
    custom_rules/          ← Your sponsor-specific rules (all .yaml files loaded)
      FLEET-AE-001.yaml
      FLEET-AE-002.yaml
      ACME-VS-001.yaml
    sdtm/
      rules/               ← CDISC CORE rules (from fleet init rules)
    adam/
      rules/

Commit the directory to VCS so the complete rule inventory is versioned alongside the study.

docs.title: ID naming convention
docs.text:
Pattern Example Owner CORE-XXXXXX CORE-000001 CDISC (official — never reuse) <COMPANY>-<DOMAIN>-<NNN> ACME-AE-001 Your organisation FLEET-<DOMAIN>-<NNN> FLEET-DM-003 Default prefix

The --prefix flag on fleet add-rule controls the prefix. Auto-increment scans existing rules in the target directory to determine the next available sequence number.

docs.title: Uniqueness guarantee
docs.text:
fleet add-rule checks all existing .yaml and .yml files in the target directory. It refuses to create a rule if the Core.Id or the file name already exists, so it never replaces a file. The engine loads .yml files too. fleet check fails when two rule files hold the same Core.Id, because the engine keeps only one of them.

fleet check-rule fails on a scaffold whose Check block still holds the placeholder VARIABLE_NAME. The scaffold has no yaml-language-server line, because that path is specific to one machine. fleet add-rule prints the line, and you can add it for schema completion in your editor.

docs.title: Validating rule schema locally
docs.text:
Before running rules through the engine, you can validate them against the vendored CDISC JSON Schema:

import json
import yaml
from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator
from pathlib import Path

schema_path = Path("src/fleet/validation/schemas/cdisc_rule_schema.json")
schema = json.loads(schema_path.read_text())

with open("metadata/custom_rules/FLEET-AE-001.yaml") as f:
    rule = yaml.safe_load(f)

validator = Draft202012Validator(schema)
errors = list(validator.iter_errors(rule))
# errors == [] means the rule is schema-valid

docs.title: Contributing upstream
docs.text: If your custom rule addresses a gap that would benefit the broader CDISC community, consider contributing it back via the CDISC Rule Editor or the CORE GitHub repository.

docs.title: How define.yaml Drives DataFrame Creation
docs.text:
define.yaml is the single source of truth for a Fleet study. One file simultaneously:

  1. Declares all output variables (fed to Define-XML 2.1 generation)
  2. Specifies how each variable is derived (executed as a pipeline)
  3. Declares codelists and controlled terminology references
  4. Defines structural metadata (keys, class, structure label)

docs.title: File Layout
docs.text:
# yaml-language-server: $schema=../../../src/fleet/define_xml/schemas/define_spec_schema.json
fleet_spec_version: 2
study:
  id:             CDISCPILOT01
  standard:       ADAMIG
  standard_version: "1.1"

codelists:
  - oid: C66731
    name: Sex
    type: text
    items:
      - coded_value: "M"
        decode: MALE
      - coded_value: "F"
        decode: FEMALE

datasets:
  - name: ADSL
    label: Subject-Level Analysis Dataset
    structure: One record per subject
    keys: [STUDYID, USUBJID]
    inputs:
      - name: DM
        type: dataset
    variables:
      - name: STUDYID
        ...

The spec is validated against the bundled JSON Schema (define_spec_schema.json), which is generated from the algorithm registry — its algorithm: enum and per-algorithm required fields always match what from_spec() actually executes (a CI sync test enforces this). The top-level fleet_spec_version: 2 pins the spec dialect; a future incompatible version is rejected with a clear message rather than silently misinterpreted.

fleet lsp reads that schema straight from the installed package, so the Fleet VS Code extension gives you inline errors with no setup. Without it, a generic YAML language server can read the same schema from a $schema comment — fleet init define prints the exact line, resolved against your install. Adding it alongside the Fleet extension reports every schema error twice, so use one or the other.

docs.title: Derivation Algorithms
docs.text:
Every spec-executable verb is declared once in the central registry (fleet.core.spec_registry), which derives the from_spec executor, the per-verb validation models and the JSON schema from the verb signature.

The verb is the algorithm (ADR-0008). A derivation: block is the verb call: the algorithm: value is the verb name and the keys are its keyword arguments. The rule for the programmer: remove .verb("TARGET", and the last ). What stays is the YAML block. Four conversions apply, because YAML has no Python objects: a Polars expression is an expression string, a frame is the name of a pinned dataset, a codelist class is its id, and a @derivation object is its registered name or dotted path. One keyword changes its spelling: else_ is written else.

Inline call Spec block .assign("DOMAIN", value="DM") algorithm: assign, value: DM .assign("SEX", source="sex", ct=SEX, ct_map={...}) algorithm: assign, source: sex, ct_map: {...} .derivation("AVAL", expression="pl.col('vs') * 2") algorithm: derivation, expression: "pl.col('vs') * 2" .derivation(AGEGR1) algorithm: derivation, callable: AGEGR1 .first_date("TRTSDT", from_dataset=ex, date_col="EXSTDTC") algorithm: first_date, from_dataset: EX, date_col: ... .case_when("ARMCD", when=[...], else_="X") algorithm: case_when, when: [...], else: X .duration("ADY", start="TRTSDT", end="ASTDT") algorithm: duration, start: TRTSDT, end: ASTDT .seq("AESEQ", by=["USUBJID"]) algorithm: seq, by: [USUBJID]

The SEX block gives no ct:: it defaults to the codelist: of the variable, so the id is written once. A ct_map on a variable with no codelist: and no ct: is a load-time error, because a mapping needs a codelist. Validation is strict in the other direction too: source and value exclude each other on assign, a derivation needs exactly one of expression and callable, and a misspelled key is rejected.

A spec written before ADR-0008 (assign_ct, hardcode_no_ct, if_then_else, ct_codelist, else_value, groups, …) fails at load. An old algorithm name gets a message that names the fix. An old key on a current algorithm (groups: on seq) gets Extra inputs are not permitted. In both cases fleet migrate --spec <define.yaml> --write rewrites the file line by line and sets fleet_spec_version: 2.

The complete, always-current list is one call away (and df.sdtm.verbs() / df.adam.verbs() gives the inline counterpart):

import fleet

print(sorted(fleet.spec_algorithms("adam")))
print(sorted(fleet.spec_algorithms("sdtm")))

docs.title: The verb-coverage matrix
docs.text:
Not every inline verb is spec-expressible. fleet.spec_coverage() returns the verb ↔ YAML keys ↔ required-keys matrix, and fleet.SPEC_UNSUPPORTED is the machine-checked allowlist of verbs that have no spec form (e.g. transform, derive_summary_records, the TDD add_* verbs) — so "which subset is spec-safe" has a definite answer instead of a guess:

import fleet

matrix = fleet.spec_coverage()  # algorithm ↔ verb ↔ required fields
inline_only = fleet.SPEC_UNSUPPORTED  # {"sdtm": {...}, "adam": {...}}
print(len(matrix), "algorithms;", len(inline_only["adam"]), "adam verbs are inline-only")

The answer covers the verbs of df.sdtm and df.adam. The verbs of the sub-namespaces (df.adam.onco, df.adam.pk, df.adam.occds and the others) are inline only in this release, except the dotted algorithms in fleet.spec_algorithms("adam") (occds.treatment_emergent). For another one, use algorithm: derivation with callable:.

docs.title: Study-specific callables (callable:)
docs.text:
When no built-in verb fits, point derivation: at a registered derivation name or a fully qualified Python dotted path. The runtime dispatch depends on the callable's kind:

  • kind="column" (zero-arg, returns pl.Expr) — stays fully lazy, no DataFrame materialisation. It writes the column named as the function, so the function name must be the variable name (or the expression ends with .alias("<variable>")); otherwise from_spec raises SpecError.
  • kind="frame" (receives upstream DataFrame, returns pl.DataFrame) — the pipeline is materialised at that point, the function is called, and the result is wrapped back into the namespace.
- name: AGEGR1
  derivation:
    algorithm: derivation
    callable: programs.derivations.AGEGR1

Or use the registered short name (if the derivations module was imported):

- name: AGEGR1
  derivation:
    callable: AGEGR1 # algorithm: derivation injected automatically

docs.title: Derivations folder convention
docs.text:
fleet derivation add AGEGR1 --dataset ADSL scaffolds a derivation file under the study's configured programs tree:

programs/derivations/       # <programs dir from study_config.yaml>
    __init__.py
    AGEGR1.py
    BMI.py

The convention is shared across standards — a callable: block works identically in SDTM and ADaM specs, because both dispatch through the same core registry and resolver. The resolver itself does no folder scanning: a callable is found either (a) by short name, when its module has been imported and the function is @derivation-registered, or (b) by fully qualified dotted path. Declare derivations_module: at the top of the spec and from_spec() imports it for you, so short names always resolve. The module is study Python that runs: from_spec() and fleet define-xml print one line on stderr (# fleet: importing study code derivations_module '...') when they import it.

Both algorithm: and callable: plug into the Define-XML methods: DefineSpecGenerator(spec) (or fleet define-xml) emits one <MethodDef> per Derived variable, named Algorithm for <VARIABLE>. The <Description> is submission text, resolved in this order:

  1. the variable's comment: — always wins;
  2. for callable: derivations, the study callable's docstring (@derivation objects use their own fn docstring) — this is study-authored text; reST markup is stripped;
  3. the registry's submission-facing template for the algorithm, with the spec params filled in (e.g. chg renders Change from baseline: AVAL - BASE.).

Fleet's verb docstrings are never used — they are API documentation, identical across studies and unstable across Fleet versions. The <FormalExpression Context="Python/Fleet"> carries the faithful call (the verb the algorithm runs plus the spec params, or the callable's dotted_path), giving a verifiable link between the regulatory submission and the exact code that produced the data. The verb is named after the public namespace class it runs on, the way the run's lineage records it in VariableNode.method, so an ADaM study_day reads fleet.adam.namespace.AdamNamespace.duration('ADY', end='ASTDT', start='TRTSDT') in the define and in the lineage of the dataset it documents. The path is importable and does not change when Fleet moves a verb between its internal mixins.

With no comment:, the template text of case_when reads each branch as "if then ", and an expression (flag criteria, derivation expression) stays verbatim. fleet define-xml warns for each variable whose method text holds a Polars expression: add a comment: in words for the reviewer.

docs.title: Example — TRTSDT (date of first dose)
docs.text:
first_date is a real spec algorithm — this example runs end to end. In the spec, from_dataset: names a pinned dataset (attach it with .pin("EX", ex) before calling from_spec); the runtime resolves the name to the pinned frame.

fleet_spec_version: 2
study:
  id: CDISCPILOT01
  standard: ADAMIG
  standard_version: "1.1"
datasets:
  - name: ADSL
    label: Subject-Level Analysis Dataset
    structure: One record per subject
    keys: [STUDYID, USUBJID]
    variables:
      - name: TRTSDT
        label: Date of First Exposure to Treatment
        type: date
        origin: Derived
        derivation:
          algorithm: first_date
          from_dataset: EX
          date_col: EXSTDTC
          # admiral template exposure rule: a placebo dose of 0 counts. The SAP decides.
          where: >-
            (pl.col("EXDOSE") > 0) | ((pl.col("EXDOSE") == 0)
            & pl.col("EXTRT").str.to_uppercase().str.contains("PLACEBO"))

Run it by pinning EX and calling from_spec (the harness writes the YAML above to define.yaml first):

import polars as pl
import fleet  # noqa: F401

dm = pl.DataFrame({"STUDYID": ["CDISCPILOT01"] * 2, "USUBJID": ["S1", "S2"]})
ex = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "USUBJID": ["S1", "S1", "S2"],
        "EXTRT": ["XANOMELINE", "XANOMELINE", "XANOMELINE"],
        "EXSTDTC": ["2014-01-05", "2014-01-02", "2014-02-01"],
        "EXDOSE": [54.0, 0.0, 54.0],  # the 0-dose active row is filtered out by where=
    }
)

adsl = dm.adam.pin("EX", ex).from_spec("define.yaml", dataset="ADSL").to_frame()
print(adsl)  # TRTSDT = 2014-01-05 for S1 (earliest dosed date), 2014-02-01 for S2

The equivalent hand-written pipeline calls the same verb directly:

treated = (
    '(pl.col("EXDOSE") > 0) | '
    '((pl.col("EXDOSE") == 0) & pl.col("EXTRT").str.to_uppercase().str.contains("PLACEBO"))'
)
adsl = dm.adam.adsl.first_date(
    "TRTSDT", from_dataset=ex, date_col="EXSTDTC", where=treated
).to_frame()

docs.title: Record filters — row_steps:
docs.text:
A step that removes records has no variable, so it does not sit in variables:. It sits in the dataset key row_steps:, in pipeline order (ADR-0034). Each step names the variable it follows with after: (null: before the first variable), and from_spec() runs it right after that variable. whereclauses keeps the records where where: is true; nodup keeps one record per subset: after the sort on order_by:.

datasets:
  - name: ADSL
    row_steps:
      - algorithm: whereclauses
        where: ARMCD != "SCRNFAIL"
        after: ARMCD
    variables:
      - name: ARMCD
        derivation: {algorithm: assign}

to_spec_yaml() writes these steps from an inline chain. A step it cannot write (a pl.Expr filter, derive_param) is written as algorithm: TODO with the verb name: from_spec() refuses the file until you write the step. Define-XML shows the steps as the dataset comment.

A variable block with algorithm: whereclauses or group_by still runs, but the variable name becomes an ItemDef that no dataset holds, so from_spec() and fleet define-xml warn: move the filter to row_steps:.

docs.title: End-to-End Flow
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[define.yaml] -->|parsed + validated| B[spec_registry]
    B -->|derivation specs| D[namespace.from_spec]
    D -->|applies verbs| E[Polars pipeline]
    E -->|calls .to_frame| F[ADSL DataFrame]
    A -->|variable metadata| C[DefineSpecGenerator]
    C --> G[define_adam.xml]
    F --> H[adsl.parquet / adsl.json]
    F --> I[DatasetChecker / ValidationService]

docs.title: Running the full pipeline programmatically
docs.text:
from_spec is the execution entry point. Pin any datasets the spec references by name, then build each dataset:

import polars as pl
import fleet  # noqa: F401

dm = pl.read_parquet("outputs/sdtm/dm.parquet")
ex = pl.read_parquet("outputs/sdtm/ex.parquet")

adsl = (
    dm.adam.pin("EX", ex)
    .from_spec("examples/cdiscpilot01/adam/define.yaml", dataset="ADSL")
    .to_frame()
)

StudyContext (via load_study_context(config_path)) resolves the configured raw_data, sdtm_data, adam_data, and metadata directories so you don't hard-code paths; it exposes sdtm_spec / adam_spec / raw_file(...) helpers.

docs.title: Generating Define-XML from the same spec
docs.text:
One CLI command — inside a study workspace, spec and output default from study_config.yaml:

uv run fleet define-xml --standard adam                 # config-based defaults
uv run fleet define-xml -s specs/define.yaml -o out.xml --strict

The same generation from Python:

from fleet import DefineSpecGenerator

DefineSpecGenerator("examples/cdiscpilot01/adam/define.yaml").generate(
    "outputs/cdiscpilot01/define_adam.xml"
)

DefineSpecGenerator emits a <MethodDef> per Derived variable (see the method text rule above); variables with origin: Collected, Assigned, Protocol, or Predecessor never reference a method. Generated documents are validated on the way out — against the vendored CDISC XSDs and a semantic lint (fleet.define_xml.semantic_errors) that rejects reviewer-facing defects such as API markup inside TranslatedText; validate_xml=False bypasses both. The lint accepts a MethodOID on a variable that is not Derived in a received define, because the CDISC Define-XML 2.1 examples use it.

docs.title: Define-XML gaps: warning or refusal
docs.text:
Define-XML 2.1 requires three things that a spec can leave out:

  • a MethodOID on each Derived ItemRef, so a Derived variable needs a comment: or a derivation: block that gives method text;
  • a Length on text, integer and float items (characters for text, digits for numbers);
  • a SignificantDigits on float items (significant_digits: in the spec, on a variable or on a value-level entry).

The generator names each gap, one line per item:

specs/define.yaml: 2 Define-XML gap(s):
  DM.SAFFL: no method text (add a comment: or a derivation: block)
  VS.AVAL (PARAMCD = SYSBP): no SignificantDigits (required on float)
Entry point A gap gives fleet define-xml, DefineSpecGenerator(spec) the file, and one warning with the list fleet define-xml --strict, DefineSpecGenerator(spec, strict=True) SpecError, exit code 1, no file fleet check a FAIL row define (sdtm) or define (adam) with the list

The schema refuses significant_digits: on a type other than float, and length: on date and datetime.

The spec keys below apply to every generation:

  • fleet_spec_version: 2 — spec dialect version (checked on load; 2 is the verb vocabulary of ADR-0008, fleet migrate --spec rewrites a version 1 file).
  • derivations_module: — a dotted module that from_spec imports itself, so callable: derivations register without a manual import. The dotted path is relative to the study root (the folder of study_config.yaml), so derivations_module: programs.derivations finds the package that fleet derivation add writes, from any working directory.
  • output_format: — per-dataset or spec-level export format (parquet, dataset-json, xpt) recorded in the DAG and Define-XML leaf hrefs, and the format fleet run writes when no --format is given.
  • output: — per-dataset Define-XML leaf href, used verbatim. It names the leaf only: fleet run still writes <name>.<ext> and warns when the two differ.
  • sdtm_role: — per-variable SDTM role (Identifier, Topic, Timing, Grouping Qualifier, Result Qualifier, Synonym Qualifier, Record Qualifier, Variable Qualifier, Rule), written as the ItemRef Role. fleet init define fills it from the CDISC Library; check a sponsor-specific role by hand (ADR 0042). It is apart from role: qualifier, which marks a Non-Standard Variable for SUPP<domain> (see Supplemental qualifiers below).
  • optional: — per-variable, for a variable with no derivation. optional: true lets fleet run write the dataset without it when no input has it (RFXSTDTC in a study that does not collect it). Without it, the run stops, so a population flag such as SAFFL is never lost with exit 0. fleet run --no-strict turns the stop into a warning for one run (ADR 0053).
  • value_level: — value-level metadata entries emitted as Define-XML <ValueListDef> / where-clause elements. where: is one condition or a list of conditions that all apply, each with an optional comparator: (EQ, NE, LT, LE, GT, GE, IN, NOTIN; default EQ for one value, IN for more). Two conditions that would get the same OID stop the generation.
  • class:, subclass:, domain: — the dataset def:Class, its def:SubClass (ADAE: ADVERSE EVENT), and the SDTM Domain of a split dataset (QSPH: QS). An ADaM dataset has no Domain. A dataset with no class warns; a class of the other model stops the generation.
  • Leaf hrefs — a Submission define that names a file other than .xpt or .json warns once. generate() copies Fleet's define2-1.xsl next to the XML when no file of that name is there; it never replaces a file.
  • ct: {validate: true, file: ...} — opt the spec into CT validation (see below).

docs.title: Codelist References
docs.text:
Variables can reference codelists declared in the codelists block:

- name: SEX
  label: Sex
  type: text
  codelist: C66731 # references the oid in codelists[]
  derivation:
    algorithm: assign
    source: SEX

The terms of a codelist decide its Define-XML form:

  • every term has a decode:: CodeListItem;
  • no term has a decode: (units, test codes): EnumeratedItem;
  • some terms have a decode: and some do not: a SpecError that names the codelist and the first term without one;
  • external: {dictionary: MedDRA, version: "26.0"} in place of items:: ExternalCodeList.

nci_code: on a codelist or a term writes the NCI Alias, and extended: true on a term marks a sponsor term (def:ExtendedValue="Yes"). A codelist whose oid is an NCI code (C66731) gets def:StandardOID="STD.CT" when study.ct_version is set; standard_oid: sets another declared standard (STD.CT.ADAM with study.adam_ct_version).

codelists:
  - oid: C66731
    name: Sex
    type: text
    nci_code: C66731
    items:
      - { coded_value: F, decode: Female, nci_code: C16576 }
      - { coded_value: X, decode: X, extended: true }
  - oid: CL.UNIT
    name: Unit
    type: text
    items: [{ coded_value: mg }, { coded_value: kg }]

Each dataset variable has its own ItemDef (IT.ADSL.AGE, IT.ADAE.AGE), so each one keeps the type, length, origin and codelist of its own dataset.

docs.title: Controlled terminology in the spec path
docs.text:
A spec step and its inline call check the same terms. Inside a study, the ct: ID of an assign, or the codelist: of its variable when ct: is absent, resolves to the class of that ID in the study's codelists.py, the module fleet init ct generates. So this entry:

- name: AESEV
  codelist: C66769
  derivation:
    algorithm: assign
    source: ae_severity

runs as .assign("AESEV", source="ae_severity", ct=AESEV) with the AESEV class of codelists.py, and a raw Mild gives the same warning in both notations: AE.AESEV: column 'ae_severity' contains values not in codelist 'C66769': ['Mild'].

  • The study is the first study_config.yaml above the folder of the define.yaml, never the working directory.
  • When the spec's ct: file: (below) or the CT loaded in fleet.get_validator() holds the codelist, it checks the values in both notations. A constant (assign with value:) is checked against the same terms as a column: the loaded CT, then the study class.
  • Outside a study, before fleet init ct, or for an ID without a class, only the loaded CT can check the values.

Because both notations then trust codelists.py, Fleet checks the file against the study:

Check Problem Fix Package A package in the __ct_packages__ or __ct_package__ marker of the file (for older files, the package in each class's _cdisc_url) is not pinned in study_config.yaml (ct.package, ct.adam_package). fleet init ct --force Mixed packages The classes name two packages of one product, for example two SDTM CT dates. An SDTM and an ADaM package together are correct. fleet init ct --force Missing codelist A codelist: or ct: ID of a define.yaml has no class in the file. fleet add-ct --domains AE (SDTM); fleet init ct --force (ADaM), after you set ct.adam_package Missing file The define.yaml files reference codelists, but the file does not exist. fleet init ct

from_spec warns once per process about all but the missing codelist, and still checks the values against the file. An inline ct= class from another package gives the package warning too. fleet check fails on all four, and fleet doctor prints one codelists.py line.

docs.title: Two CT packages: SDTM CT and ADaM CT
docs.text:
CDISC publishes ADaM CT on its own dates, and some codelists are only in ADaM CT (DTYPE, C81224). A study with ADaM datasets pins both packages in study_config.yaml:

ct:
  package: sdtmct-2023-12-15
  adam_package: adamct-2023-06-30
  • fleet init cfg and fleet new with ADaM datasets pin adamct-2023-06-30, the latest ADaM CT package on or before the default SDTM package. With another --package, give --adam-package too.
  • fleet init ct takes each codelist from the first pinned package that holds it, SDTM CT first. When no pinned package holds a codelist, it names the ID, writes no file and exits with code 1.
  • fleet init ct also writes the terms and decodes (the NCI preferred term) into each codelists: entry of the define.yaml files that has no terms yet; with --force, into every entry. The file is rewritten, so only its header comment stays. A Define-XML CodeList needs its terms, and fleet define-xml names each codelist without them.
  • The ADaM define.yaml states both dates: ct_version (SDTM CT, for SEX) and adam_ct_version (ADaM CT, for DTYPE). Its Define-XML lists two CT standards, with the publishing sets SDTM and ADaM.

docs.title: Opting the spec into CT validation
docs.text:
Without a top-level ct: block, an assign with a codelist and without ct_map checks its values (pass-through), and one with ct_map maps them without a check. Add a top-level ct: block to check every assign with a codelist, mapped ones included; out-of-codelist values emit a warning naming the dataset, variable, and codelist:

ct:
  validate: true
  file: ct/cdisc_ct.yaml   # optional — loaded for this spec only, also without validate:
datasets:
  - name: DM
    variables:
      - name: SEX
        codelist: C66731
        derivation:
          algorithm: assign
          source: sex

When datasets are checked with DatasetChecker(spec, check_ct=True), the values are also verified against the spec's own inline codelists:, and codelist lookups are normalised to concept IDs — so a spec cannot ship values that contradict the conformance it asserts in the generated Define-XML.

docs.title: Schema Validation — What, When, and How
docs.text: Fleet has two independent layers of schema validation for define.yaml. They run at different points and catch different classes of error.

docs.title: Layer 1 — Registry model validation (pipeline-build time)
docs.text:
When you call .from_spec(), Fleet resolves each variable's algorithm: through the spec registry and validates its derivation block against a discriminated-union Pydantic model generated for that algorithm. The model declares exactly which fields are required and sets extra="forbid", so a misspelled field is a loud error — not a silent column of nulls. This runs immediately when .from_spec() is called, before any data is materialised.

What it catches:

  • Unknown algorithm names (with a did-you-mean suggestion)
  • Misspelled or unexpected fields (extra="forbid")
  • Missing required fields for a given algorithm
  • Wrong field types (e.g. a list where a string is expected)

Errors are wrapped in a SpecError that names file → dataset → variable. Here is the real message for a typo'd key (ct_mp instead of ct_map):

# derivation block with a typo:
#   - name: SEX
#     codelist: C66731
#     derivation:
#       algorithm: assign
#       source: sex
#       ct_mp: {"F": "F"}         # ← typo: should be ct_map

dm = raw_df.sdtm.from_spec("specs/define.yaml", dataset="DM")
# fleet.core.exceptions.SpecError:
# specs/define.yaml → dataset DM → variable SEX: 1 validation error for SDTMAssignSpec
# ct_mp
#   Extra inputs are not permitted [type=extra_forbidden, input_value={'F': 'F'}, input_type=dict]

(Note: an assign with a codelist id that no loaded CT holds does not error — it copies the value through and emits a UserWarning that CT could not be validated. assign never fabricates a missing-field error for an optional key.)

docs.title: Layer 2 — Define-XML generation in strict mode (fleet check)
docs.text:
fleet check generates the Define-XML of every define.yaml the study config points at, in strict mode, and writes no file. The row passes only when the generator gives a valid document. This layer fires on demand, not automatically during pipeline execution.

uv run fleet check

What it catches:

  • a spec that does not conform to define_spec_schema.json (SpecSchemaError, with the path of the bad entry);
  • a codelist: reference to a codelist that the spec does not declare;
  • a key, a value-level variable or a where-clause variable that its dataset does not declare, and a crf_pages document that study.documents does not declare;
  • in an SDTMIG 3.4 (or earlier) spec, a role: qualifier variable that cannot move to its generated SUPP<domain> (see Supplemental qualifiers below). The message names SUPP<domain> and the reason;
  • a study.ct_version (or adam_ct_version) that is not the date of the CT package that study_config.yaml pins;
  • a Define-XML gap: method text, Length or SignificantDigits (see Define-XML gaps above);
  • a generated document that fails the CDISC XSDs or the semantic lint.

fleet check imports no study code: it does not import the derivations_module of the spec, and a callable: derivation is described by its comment: or its dotted path. fleet define-xml imports the module to write the method text of each callable:.

The derivation blocks themselves are checked by layer 1: the verb's model knows the required keys, so there are no separate per-algorithm rules.

The same check from Python: DefineSpecGenerator(path, strict=True).to_xml_string() raises on the first of these problems and returns the XML text otherwise.

docs.title: When to run each layer
docs.text: Layer When it fires Blocks execution? Registry models Automatically on .from_spec() call Yes — raises SpecError (file → dataset → variable) fleet check Manually or in CI, before submission Yes — a FAIL row and exit code 1 CDISC Rules Engine Manually, after datasets are materialised No — report only

docs.title: JSON Schema & Editor Support
docs.text:
The YAML spec is validated against the bundled schema at:

src/fleet/define_xml/schemas/define_spec_schema.json

This schema is generated from the algorithm registry — its algorithm: enum, per-algorithm required fields, and the fleet_spec_version / derivations_module properties are derived from the same declarations that drive execution, and a CI test fails if the checked-in schema drifts. The schema checks keys, types and required fields. from_spec() also checks the exclusive groups (source or value on assign) and the codelist rule, so some errors appear only at run time. Regenerate it after registry changes with:

uv run python -m fleet.define_xml.schema_builder

Add this comment to the top of every spec file to activate YAML language-server auto-complete in VS Code or any LSP-enabled editor:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=../../../src/fleet/define_xml/schemas/define_spec_schema.json

docs.title: Supplemental qualifiers
docs.text:
An SDTM variable with role: qualifier (or algorithm: nsv) is a Non-Standard Variable. fleet run builds it, then moves it to a SUPP<domain> dataset (SDTMIG 3.4 section 8.4) and writes the parent without it. IDVAR is <domain>SEQ; only DM may have no IDVAR, so another domain with no --SEQ stops the run. Later datasets of the same run still read the qualifier from the full frame.

The same define.yaml gives the Define-XML. For SDTMIG 3.4 or earlier, fleet define-xml and fleet check leave the qualifier out of the parent ItemGroupDef and add a SUPP<domain> ItemGroupDef (ADR 0044):

  • the variables STUDYID, RDOMAIN, USUBJID, IDVAR, IDVARVAL, QNAM, QLABEL, QVAL, QORIG and QEVAL, with the keys STUDYID, RDOMAIN, USUBJID, IDVAR, IDVARVAL and QNAM;
  • value-level metadata on QVAL: one where clause QNAM EQ <name> per qualifier, with its label, type, length, codelist, origin and method;
  • IDVAR text <domain>SEQ (for DM: null), the rule of fleet run;
  • the leaf supp<domain> in the format of the parent.
- name: AE
  variables:
    - name: AESEQ
      # ...
    - name: AETRTEM
      label: Treatment Emergent Flag
      type: text
      length: 1
      origin: Derived
      role: qualifier  # fleet run: SUPPAE; define: IG.SUPPAE, QVAL where QNAM EQ AETRTEM
      derivation:
        algorithm: assign
        source: trtem
